content:
The first version put the CV and a few posts online with Hugo. This rebuild gives the CV, articles and repository notes a shared visual identity, while keeping a layout suited to each kind of reading. It follows Create a portfolio with Hugo (week 1).
Project architecture overview. Open the image to inspect the details.
1. A shared canvas, with room for the content The slate-blue background and pale paper surface now connect the CV to the blog. Teal marks links, selected filters and useful actions. Fraunces carries the main titles; body text and controls use more restrained type. The palette, spacing and motion rules are recorded in DESIGN.md[1].
The same identity has different proportions on each page. The CV puts the name, portrait and PDF action first. An article needs a comfortable reading column and clear sections. A project reference needs room for commands, API tables and diagrams, with page navigation beside it on a wide screen.
On a narrow screen, navigation and actions wrap, long code scrolls inside its own block, and the text remains in one column. Figures keep their full contents visible. A surface plot or architecture diagram loses meaning when its axes or labels are cropped.
2. Owning the Paper overrides The blog moved from HBTheme to Paper[2]. Project templates in hugo/layouts/ define the article header, lists, search and project pages. Shared styles live in hugo/assets/.
This makes a template fix apply across articles. The header now groups the content kind, date, reading time and topic badges. Longer articles have a collapsible contents list. English and French remain paired by translationKey, with the language switcher in the site header. Repeating a translation link in each introduction adds another navigation choice to a paragraph that should introduce the subject.
The article description stays in search and social metadata. The visible opening is the article’s first paragraph, so readers encounter the introduction once.
3. Articles and project references have different jobs The post_kind field distinguishes articles, conferences and tutorials in lists and search. Recipes keep their own section. Repository pages live under projects/notes/, where the catalog can link to a stable technical reference.
An article can follow one idea through the code. Its project note holds setup commands, source references and optional API or deployment details. For example, a Docker project needs service ports, storage and startup relationships. A numerical library needs its data structures and the path into its algorithms. Empty sections make both harder to read.
The catalog supports searching and combining filters. Documentation and GitHub remain separate actions on each card. Archive and fork badges describe repository status; they do not replace the project’s title or summary.
4. Diagrams should be useful at the reading size Mermaid diagrams now have zoom, Fit, full-size, fullscreen and SVG export controls. A diagram starts fitted to the available space. Readers can then inspect a particular label without scrolling the whole page sideways.
Text and source links still explain the relationships. In deployment diagrams, a dependency arrow needs a precise meaning: Compose’s depends_on records startup order, while readiness is a separate concern.
flowchart TB Source["Files in git"] --> CV["English and French CV"] Source --> Posts["Paired Markdown articles"] Source --> Notes["Repository notes and data"] Posts --> Hugo["Paper and Hugo overrides"] Notes --> Hugo CV --> Build["Local production build"] Hugo --> Build Build --> Pages["Published static site"] The earlier stack diagram source records the theme and editorial tools used during the rebuild.
5. Skills make editing rules explicit I use repository skills to keep recurring changes consistent. cv-hero identifies the canonical CV pages and their generated English copy. hugo-site describes the templates, bilingual page bundles and navigation. project-docs specifies the repository-note structure and the evidence needed for technical claims.
The Apple design guidance helps review hierarchy, target sizes, contrast and motion. For this website, those principles apply to browser controls and responsive layouts. The humanizer pass focuses on the writing: direct explanations, concrete details and fewer repeated introductions.
These skills give an editor a place to look before changing a shared component. The result still needs review against the actual page. A rule cannot tell whether a chosen image belongs to the project or whether a diagram’s labels are legible.
6. Previewing and publishing The source remains in git: HTML for the CV, paired Markdown bundles for articles, and data files for repository references. The JSON Resume article explains the machine-readable CV alongside those pages.
I build the production output locally, check the generated pages, and publish the static tree. The last-updated labels use the release date in America/Toronto. Original article dates keep their historical meaning.
A preview needs more than a successful build. I check light and dark mode, small and wide viewports, language links, image loading and the controls that a reader can use. Reduced-motion settings also need to leave every piece of content accessible. The slide-deck preview now serves rendered slides locally, which lets it work during development as well as after publication.
7. Related reading Create a portfolio with Hugo (week 1) Software engineering journey
summary: Rebuilding my Hugo portfolio: shared visual identity, bilingual articles, repository skills, interactive diagrams and local publication.
title: Website refonte with Hugo (part 2)

content:
AINewsTracker turns financial news into records that can be searched, analysed and compared with market data.
The project is a FastAPI service with separate routes for news, articles, companies, users, data seeding and trading strategies. Routes receive HTTP requests; services and repositories handle analysis and storage.
1. From a feed to an article A news request starts a collection job. The news service retrieves feed content and creates article records. The metrics service analyses the text, and the article repository stores the result in MongoDB.
Responsibility Source file Receive the request app/routers/news.py Collect news app/core/services/news.py Analyse the text app/core/services/metrics.py Store articles app/core/repo/article.py Routes describe the API surface, models define stored data, services perform the news work, and repositories isolate database access. app/main.py also configures Redis caching.
AlgoETS. (n.d.). Article processing flow. AINewsTracker repository, docs/diagrams/out/article_processing_flow.svg.
Original processing diagram[1].
2. Keep the source attached to the analysis The documentation’s data overview[2] connects four records: a news source produces articles, comments belong to an article, and company records identify the businesses it mentions. Source metadata includes language and country. Articles retain their URL, publication date and text alongside analysis fields.
That separation makes a result easier to inspect. A sentiment label can be traced to an article and its publisher. A company’s ticker provides a way to connect mentions across articles without treating every spelling of its name as a different business.
3. What the text analysis produces The documented NLP outputs include a sentiment label and score, ticker detections, a summary and topic labels. These fields answer different reading questions: which company is discussed, what the article says, and how its language is classified. The documentation’s sample records illustrate the model; the Pydantic classes define the actual fields.
I would inspect the original text beside those outputs before using them as strategy inputs. A summary can omit a condition, and a company mention does not establish that the article concerns a tradable event. The source URL and publication date therefore belong in the review path.
4. Analysis and backtesting The project documentation describes sentiment analysis, topic classification, ticker allocation and article summarisation. The strategy route sends backtest requests to app/core/trading/strategy.py.
These labels are inputs to an experiment. They do not prove that a news item caused a market move, and a historical backtest does not guarantee future performance.
A useful review separates the data stages:
Stage What to inspect Collection Publisher, source URL, publication time and retrieved text Text analysis Detected companies, labels and summary against the original article Strategy input Which observations were available at the point being tested Backtest output The chosen period, assumptions and the strategy’s reported result This review checks the data available to the strategy, its assumptions and its reported result. The article presents no measured prediction accuracy or trading returns.
5. Read the architecture The complete GitDiagram includes route registrations, models, repositories, seeders, MongoDB, Redis and the trading branch. Each node links to its source file.
Interactive GitDiagram[3] AINewsTracker project reference Source repository[4] Published documentation[5] Data model and NLP overview[2]
summary: Following financial news from collection to analysis and historical backtesting with AINewsTracker.
title: Following financial news through AINewsTracker

content:
IPC Toolkit is a C++ library for contact calculations. It provides collision detection, distance derivatives and friction potentials. The application supplies the time-stepping loop and solver.
1. Where it fits A simulation passes collision geometry and vertex motion to the contact library. The diagram follows that query through broad-phase candidates and narrow-phase continuous collision detection (CCD), then back to the application.
A contact query starts and ends in the calling simulation. Time stepping and solving remain the application’s responsibility.
2. What it computes The routines cover several parts of contact handling:
Area Available calculations Collision detection Broad- and narrow-phase continuous collision detection. Distance Distance derivatives for edges and triangles. Contact barriers Barrier functions and derivatives, distance barrier potentials, and adaptive barrier stiffness. Friction Smooth or lagged dissipative friction potentials. IPC Toolkit is not a complete physics engine. The upstream project points to PolyFEM and Rigid IPC as complete simulation implementations that use the library.
3. My contributions The fork at antoinebou12/ipc-toolkit[1] is where I stage changes before proposing them upstream. The pull requests below are the public record (GitHub, retrieved 2026-11-05); status is as GitHub reports it.
Pull request Opened Status ipc-sim/ipc-toolkit #210 — Anisotropic friction[2] 2026-02 Merged 2026-04-16 ipc-sim/ipc-toolkit #208 — Option to pass parameters to the Scalable CCD narrow phase[3] 2026-01 Merged 2026-01-26 ipc-sim/ipc-toolkit #144 — Draft adhesion documentation[4] 2024-11 Merged 2024-12-11 ipc-sim/ipc-toolkit #139 — Static and kinetic coefficients in the tangential collision force[5] 2024-11 Closed without merge ipc-sim/ipc-toolkit #128 — Pairwise kinetic and static friction for different materials[6] 2024-11 Closed without merge Continuous-Collision-Detection/Scalable-CCD #5 — Remove -fpic for the Windows CUDA build (vcpkg)[7] 2024-09 Merged 2024-09-27 Continuous-Collision-Detection/Scalable-CCD #6 — Multiple CUDA version tests[8] 2024-09 Closed without merge Two staging pull requests remain open on the fork: #3 — extract tolerance and max iterations from TightInclusionCCD for GPU CCD[9] and #4 — anisotropic friction[10], the branch behind upstream #210.
The thread through these changes is friction that depends on direction and material pair, which is what my thesis work on surface wear needed from the contact model, plus the GPU continuous-collision-detection path (Scalable CCD) that the Windows build and the parameter pass-through unblocked.
4. Read the code and build instructions The project documentation covers the repository structure. Use the upstream README[11] for build instructions and the contributor fork[1] for changes in that fork.
summary: How IPC Toolkit supplies collision detection, distance derivatives and friction calculations to a simulation.
title: IPC Toolkit: collision and friction inside a simulation

content:
MistubaVideo turns simulation exports into images and video with Mitsuba 3. Its batch renderer handles OBJ sequences; the mitsuba-video helper replays recorded body poses and surface fields such as wear.
1. Where rendering fits A simulation computes motion and changes to surfaces. The renderer reads those outputs to show where bodies moved, which regions of the UV atlas changed, and how the material appearance evolves. Rendering a recording lets you change the camera or lighting without repeating the simulation.
python main.py multi --folder exports renders an OBJ sequence. Camera views, resolution and samples per pixel control the output; FFmpeg assembles the images into video or GIF. The field renderer adds per-frame transforms and textures.
Existing material illustration from the project report. It illustrates shading, without representing a wear-simulation result.
2. The render helper Stage Data Input Meshes, materials, recorded poses and surface fields Processing Source adapter, material blend and Mitsuba rendering Output Rendered frames, area CSV, settings and MP4 The mitsuba-video package accepts a versioned manifest or a TextureFriction recording through a source adapter. A manifest describes bodies, meshes, materials, poses and field images. ManifestWriter lets another simulator export this format.
For each selected frame, the helper applies recorded poses, blends base and affected materials using the surface field, and renders the scene. It can add a heatmap, a UV-atlas panel and a covered-area chart before encoding an MP4.
flowchart TD subgraph Inputs[Simulation output] R[TextureFriction recording] M[Manifest: meshes, poses and fields] end subgraph Helper[mitsuba-video helper] A[Source adapter] B[Apply poses and blend materials] C[Mitsuba 3 path tracing] D[Atlas panel and area chart] end R --> A M --> A A --> B --> C --> D D --> E[Frame images and MP4] Start with inspect to check the input and preview to check framing. render produces the sequence; encode changes video assembly using existing frames. Quality presets include preview, draft and paper.
mitsuba-video inspect path/to/manifest.json mitsuba-video preview path/to/manifest.json mitsuba-video render path/to/manifest.json -q preview 3. Reading the output Outputs include beauty images, composite frames, a field-area CSV and render_config.json with settings and timings. Linear EXR frames are optional. The chart measures the recorded field’s covered area. It does not measure the visible area of the rendered object.
Keep display settings with the render when comparing videos: changing the heatmap range can make the same field look different.
Existing lighting illustration from the report. Scene lighting and the recorded surface field are separate inputs.
4. Sources and tests The package documents pytest tests for transforms, material blending, OBJ and MTL readers, and the manifest schema and writer. A measured coverage percentage is not supplied here.
Render-helper documentation[1].
Implementation: source interface[2], material blending[3].
The project documentation provides the source link and terminology.
MistubaVideo on GitHub[4]
summary: From recorded body poses and surface fields to rendered frames, heatmaps and video.
title: MistubaVideo: rendering simulation recordings with Mitsuba

content:
TrueMapData reads surface captures from TrueMap and GelSight, exposes their heights as NumPy arrays, and provides tools for analysis and graphics export. The same surface representation supports metrology work and assets such as displacement maps or meshes.
1. What a capture contains A .tmd file contains a header, spatial metadata and a grid of heights. The library supports the legacy v1 format and the TrueMap v6-style v2 format. Both store float32 samples in row-major order: height_map[row, column], with shape (height, width). Scan lengths and offsets describe the capture’s physical extent.
That metadata matters when a grid leaves the file reader. A texture can stretch over any UV range; a measured surface needs its sample spacing to retain physical scale. The binary format guide[1] documents the byte layout and the reader’s checks for alternate v2 headers.
from tmd import TMD capture = TMD.load("path/to/capture.tmd") heights = capture.height_map metadata = capture.metadata The path above is a placeholder for a capture. The code reads the raster and metadata together.
2. Inspect the surface before exporting it The visualization commands offer a 2D heatmap, a 3D surface, row and column profiles, contours, and comparisons between files. Matplotlib produces static plots; Plotly can save an interactive HTML view. Optional Polyscope support provides a 3D inspection window.
A profile shows how height varies across one section of a surface. Source: TrueMapData README visual examples.
pip install "truemapdata[viz]" tmd-process visualize basic path/to/capture.tmd tmd-process visualize 3d path/to/capture.tmd --plotter plotly --output surface.html I check the height field and its scale before choosing a derived map. A normal map describes local orientation for shading. A displacement map carries height information. Mesh export creates geometry in formats including STL, OBJ, PLY, glTF and USD, with the optional mesh dependencies installed.
flowchart TB Capture["TrueMap or GelSight capture"] --> Read["Height grid and spatial metadata"] Read --> Inspect["Heatmap, profile or 3D surface"] Inspect --> Metrics["Roughness and surface metrics"] Inspect --> Maps["Normal and displacement maps"] Inspect --> Mesh["Mesh export and template texturing"] The apply-on-mesh path bundles derived textures with a template OBJ/MTL. It uses template bounds, mm_per_pixel and capture dimensions to set tiling. This connects the size of the scan to the surface receiving the texture.
3. Roughness and wear answer different questions Roughness analysis describes a surface at a particular capture. The optional truemapdata[roughness] extra uses Surfalize for ISO 25178 areal parameters. Surfalize is GPL-3.0 and is installed separately from the MIT-licensed core package.
Wear analysis compares captures over time. Before subtracting heights, the frames need the same grid and the same in-plane region. The sequence guide[2] describes translation alignment and OpenCV/SIFT registration, including registration driven by normals.
The loss convention is reference height − current height. Positive loss means the current surface is lower than the reference. Computing a physical volume also needs the pixel spacing in both directions. Registration errors or inconsistent height units would change that result.
The tmd-wear commands cover volume series, scratch evolution, slip-axis heuristics and roughness trajectories. Those outputs complement the filters, defect detection, sequence export and compression tools in tmd-process.
4. Source and examples The surface and profile figures here are original examples from the repository README[3], not measurements from my thesis. The surface figure uses normalized heights.
The TrueMapData project note links the repository and its code overview.
TrueMapData repository[4] Documentation[5] Visualization guide[6]
summary: TrueMapData connects TrueMap and GelSight files to visualisation, surface metrics, wear analysis and mesh export.
title: TrueMapData: from measured height maps to usable assets

content:
Dimension is my Rust workspace for mathematics and graphics experiments. The useful starting point is mathlib: it exposes matrix storage, numerical solvers and the transformations that the rendering crate uses on the CPU.
Project architecture overview. Open the image to inspect the details.
1. Architecture flowchart LR Geometry["Geometry"] --> Math["CPU transforms<br/>mathlib"] Math --> Scene["Scene and cameras"] Scene --> Render["wgpu renderer"] Render --> Native["Native window"] Render --> Web["Web canvas"] The application supplies geometry and transforms. The scene layer organizes entities and cameras; the rendering layer prepares the GPU work for a native window or web canvas. This is the rendering path, not a claim that every numerical operation runs on the GPU.
Open the component-by-component code walkthrough.
2. Start with the storage mathlib/src/lib.rs[1] exports dense storage alongside sparse formats such as CRS and CCS. The public API also includes matrix and vector types, matrix views and submatrices. Those choices matter before a renderer draws anything: they determine how a caller represents and passes its data.
The same entry point exposes LU, Cholesky and SVD decompositions, plus root finding and numerical integration. Optional GPU functionality sits behind a feature flag. The presence of an executor abstraction is a design choice, not a measured speedup; I have not included performance comparisons here.
3. Follow a transform into the scene render/src/lib.rs[2] describes a wgpu renderer that uses mathlib for CPU transforms and camera mathematics. Its exports include World, EntityId, Transform, cameras and render targets.
The scene represents parent-child relationships with a tree. A local transform therefore belongs to a hierarchy: moving a parent changes the context in which its children are rendered. Serialization is optional and enabled through the serde feature.
The platform layer supports native windows and WebAssembly canvas targets. Keeping platform code apart from scene and numerical code gives those targets shared building blocks, although it does not prove identical behavior on every GPU or browser.
4. Read the workspace, not only the README The root Cargo.toml[3] lists crates for rendering, geometry, collision, kinematics, physics, networking, parsing and neural work alongside mathlib. The README still focuses on the mathematics crate. I use the manifest and module entry points to understand the current structure.
This is exploratory code. Performance comparisons would need a reproducible benchmark with its input size and target hardware.
Browse Dimension on GitHub[4].
summary: Inside my Dimension workspace: matrix storage, numerical methods, scene transforms and a wgpu renderer for native and web targets.
title: Dimension: connecting Rust mathematics to a renderer

content:
I started DasherControl because my homelab services kept spreading across browser tabs. The idea was a workspace of applets: bookmarks and embedded applications arranged in a dashboard, with a few Docker controls nearby.
1. Two paths behind the same dashboard flowchart LR Dashboard["Dashboard"] --> Workspace["Save workspace"] Workspace --> Database[("Workspace records")] Dashboard --> Action["Container action"] Action --> Docker["Docker via Shiplift"] Saving a layout goes through workspace handlers and database records. Restarting a container goes through the Shiplift adapter to Docker. PostgreSQL does not execute the Docker action, and an applet is not itself a running container. Keeping those paths separate helps explain both permissions and failure states.
Follow the handlers and Docker boundary in the architecture note.
2. A workspace has an owner The frontend uses Vue, while the backend uses Rust, Rocket and Diesel. In src/workspaces/handler.rs[1], the list handler reads the tenant identifier from a token. The handler that returns applets checks the workspace’s tenant before returning its contents.
The create-with-applets route also derives the tenant identifier from the token. That is the intended ownership model: a saved layout belongs to a user, and applets belong to a workspace.
The file contains older create and delete paths with different checks. Their presence is a reason to inspect authorization across every operation before using this as a shared service. This article describes an experiment, not a security review of a deployed system.
3. Docker is a separate boundary src/containers/docker.rs[2] wraps Shiplift calls for listing containers and images, pulling images, creating containers, and stopping or restarting them. This separates the dashboard’s workspace model from Docker operations.
It also exposes a UI problem: the list helpers return an empty vector after a Docker error. An empty dashboard could therefore mean either “nothing is running” or “the service could not be reached.” I would make those states visibly different in a new version.
4. What the browser can embed The README records iframe login failures. Applications can restrict embedding, and authentication inside a frame may behave differently from an ordinary tab. A dashboard needs an external link for those services even when an iframe works for others.
This is an older project. The repository’s screenshot and optional GIF preserve the interface as it was; they do not demonstrate compatibility with current dependencies.
Play the original demo GIF Browse the source and original README[3]. Both illustrations come from its images directory.
summary: A look back at DasherControl: Vue applets, Rust and Rocket handlers, persisted workspaces and a Docker interface.
title: DasherControl: a homelab dashboard built around workspaces

content:
My bloc repository[1] is a fork of MrKuros/Blender-Cloud-Storage[2]. It keeps the upstream author credit and explores a Blender panel for browsing assets in AWS S3 and MinIO.
1. The browsing and import paths flowchart LR Storage["S3 or MinIO"] --> Listing["Folder listing"] Listing --> Panel["Blender panel"] Panel --> Download["Download selected asset"] Download --> Import["Local Blender importer"] Listing creates the panel’s folder view; loading an asset downloads its bytes and invokes a local importer. A listing refresh can therefore succeed while an import fails on an unsupported format. The background refresh hands UI updates back through Blender timers instead of treating the storage request as a UI operation.
Read the architecture note with the connection and import boundaries.
2. Make the connection explicit addon.py[3] defines a CloudConnection property group with a provider, endpoint, bucket and region. Preferences hold multiple connections and an active connection index. The client setup chooses the S3 or MinIO path from that selection.
This is the part that interests me as both graphics and platform work: the artist works inside Blender, while the add-on translates those actions into object-storage operations.
3. Turn object names into folders Object storage uses keys. The refresh operator splits those keys on / and builds a nested dictionary for the panel. Folder expansion is tracked separately, so the UI can browse a hierarchy without pretending it is a local filesystem.
CloudSearchManager adds fuzzy matching with RapidFuzz. It scores filenames and path segments, gives direct substring matches priority and supports filters for scenes, meshes, images and materials.
4. Downloading and importing are different actions The download helper saves an object to a temporary local path. The load operator then selects a Blender importer for STL, OBJ, PLY or USD variants. Other extensions are rejected with a message. A successful transfer alone does not mean Blender has imported a usable object.
The upload-current-file operator sends the saved .blend file. Although the README discusses dependencies, I would verify texture packaging and relative paths before relying on this path to move a complete scene.
5. Keep the fork’s scope visible The public upstream comparison[4] showed 10 commits ahead and 5 behind on October 23, 2026. The changed files include the add-on, packaging metadata and README. That describes repository history; it does not establish that upstream accepted those changes.
The source also uses a single S3 list_objects_v2 request, so buckets beyond one response need pagination work. These are the kinds of small workflow boundaries I want to keep visible when revisiting the project.
summary: A code tour of my Blender cloud-storage fork: multiple connections, folder browsing, fuzzy search and mesh imports.
tags_text: Blender Python S3 MinIO Open source
title: My bloc fork: browsing S3 and MinIO from Blender

content:
My reverse-proxy project uses Caddy on a DigitalOcean VPS, with Cloudflare DNS. Terraform creates the infrastructure, Ansible configures it, and separate checks examine the resulting service.
This article describes the repository as reviewed on October 22, 2026. The source is private, so the diagram is deliberately simplified and contains no real domains, addresses or credentials. I reviewed the code without running a deployment.
1. Two kinds of change Terraform manages the infrastructure layer. The DNS configuration defines apex and wildcard records, including IPv6 variants. Ansible handles the server and application configuration. A justfile provides entry points for provisioning, deployment and validation.
flowchart TD A[Local task runner or CI] --> T[Terraform] T --> V[DigitalOcean VPS] T --> D[Cloudflare DNS records] V --> N[Ansible configuration] N --> C[Caddy container] C --> S[Upstream applications] N --> B[Configuration backup] N --> Q[Configuration validation] Q --> H[Deployment diagnostics] The arrows describe responsibilities, not a guarantee that every command follows the same path. The important boundary is ownership: DNS changes should not be independently managed by two automation systems.
2. Read the deployment order The Caddy role starts with backup tasks, optionally prepares a CrowdSec bouncer, sets up the container, and then includes configuration-validation tasks. Those tasks check endpoint structure and TLS-provider references. For example, an endpoint needs a hostname and an upstream, redirect or wildcard configuration.
That catches a different class of problem from an HTTP probe. A configuration can be structurally valid while its upstream application is unavailable. Conversely, an existing service can still answer requests while a proposed configuration is invalid.
The repository also contains roles for Umami analytics, WireGuard and system setup. Their presence does not mean every deployment enables all of them.
3. A response is not the same as a healthy application The health-check task file includes container, admin API, HTTP, HTTPS, metrics and certificate diagnostics. Several checks intentionally avoid failing the playbook. Some accept responses such as 404, 502 or 503 as well as successful status codes.
Those responses can establish that a proxy is reachable. They cannot establish that a user-facing application works. A useful deployment gate needs an expected response from the relevant application, not simply any response from the proxy.
There is another distinction worth keeping visible: the reviewed role entry point does not directly include the health-check task file. Its deployment summary leaves several health fields unset. A task file existing in a repository is not evidence that a particular deployment executed it.
4. Backup is a prerequisite, not a rollback guarantee The rollback tasks look for an available configuration backup, restore it when possible and attempt to restart the container. The role entry point places its rescue block after earlier task includes. I would not describe that as automatic recovery from every deployment failure.
For future changes, the checks I want are concrete: a known-good backup, a tested restoration path, explicit application-level health criteria, and a failure that actually stops promotion. This review does not claim those improvements have already been implemented.
Source basis: the private repository README, Terraform DNS resource declarations, and Caddy role entry-point, validation, health-check and rollback tasks. Operational configuration and secrets are omitted.
summary: A code-based look at my Caddy infrastructure: Terraform for VPS and DNS, Ansible for configuration, and the limits of deployment health checks.
title: My reverse proxy: separating provisioning, configuration and health checks

content:
antoinebou12/Artemis-Switch ★ 36 · 2 forks · Repository created 2026-08-08
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-11-05. A stream can report a healthy bitrate and still feel late. Artemis Switch is my Moonlight-Switch fork for Nintendo Switch, focused on the path between receiving a frame and presenting it. The useful question is not just “how fast is the decoder?” but “where did this frame wait?”
1. A client with a clear boundary Artemis builds on XITRIX/Moonlight-Switch: Borealis for the interface, the Moonlight/GameStream protocol for transport, FFmpeg/NVDEC for decoding, and deko3d for Switch presentation. Sunshine and Apollo remain PC hosts. Host administration stays in their own interfaces.
This distinction matters when debugging. A wrong virtual-display mode is a host issue; a growing decoded-frame queue belongs to the client. The repository documents host integrations, but that is not evidence that every host/device combination has passed hardware validation.
2. The frame pipeline flowchart TD H["PC host: Sunshine or Apollo"] --> N["Moonlight / GameStream transport"] N --> D["FFmpeg / NVDEC decode"] D --> Q["Decoded-frame queue"] Q --> S["Deadline and freshness selection"] S --> R["deko3d presentation"] R --> P["Switch display"] T["FramePipelineTelemetry"] -. measures .-> D T -. measures .-> Q T -. measures .-> R This is a simplified reading of the streaming code, not a claim about measured end-to-end input latency.
3. The subtle part: when to discard old frames LowLatencyFrameSelection.hpp[1] checks the oldest frame’s deadline before advancing to the newest frame. Once the queue is eligible, it discards older frames and favors freshness. A backlog can bypass the ordinary gate so a stalled renderer catches up.
Why preserve that oldest deadline? If the gate follows the newest arriving frame, its deadline can keep moving forward. The queue receives frames, yet presentation starves. This small policy is more informative than a generic “low latency” label.
4. Measure stages separately FramePipelineTelemetry.hpp[2] records decode timing, queue wait, client pipeline timing, render and GPU submission cost, actual video bitrate, and first-packet/decode/present milestones. It uses a monotonic clock and protects shared state with a mutex.
“Client pipeline” begins after network completion in this implementation. It does not include every host encoding, network transit, display scanout, and controller delay.
The README also describes Fit/Fill/Stretch presentation, FSR-style upscaling, RCAS sharpening, named stream profiles, and a performance overlay. These are controls to investigate tradeoffs, not a universal FPS promise.
5. What I would compare on hardware Keep the host, scene, resolution, and network fixed. Compare queue wait and present intervals with pacing options changed one at a time. Then test handheld and docked presentation separately. A lower average with worse spikes may still feel worse.
The project remains active. Its README explicitly separates portable tests and release builds from device validation. Read the installation and status notes[3] before treating a compile result as a gameplay result.
6. Source trail Repository and screenshots[4] Frame selection policy[1] Pipeline telemetry[2] Earlier handheld project overview
summary: Inside Artemis Switch: Moonlight transport, NVDEC, deko3d, frame pacing and the telemetry that makes streaming delays easier to diagnose.
title: Artemis Switch: following a frame from the network to the screen

content:
antoinebou12/ComfyUI-UML ★ 3 · 3 forks · Repository created 2026-02-23
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. ComfyUI is useful beyond image generation when an intermediate result can become a node output. ComfyUI-UML applies that idea to diagrams: text enters a rendering node; an image, a saved file, and a shareable URL can leave it.
1. Keep the source in the workflow A screenshot is hard to revise. Mermaid or PlantUML source is much easier to inspect, compare, and regenerate. The node lets that source travel with the rest of a ComfyUI workflow instead of becoming an unexplained image.
The README documents 28 Kroki diagram types, with output formats validated per type. This does not mean every renderer supports every format.
flowchart TD T["Diagram text or optional LLM output"] --> N["Normalize diagram source"] N --> U["UMLDiagram node"] U --> K["Kroki web renderer"] U --> L["Optional local Mermaid / Graphviz"] K --> O["Image, file and URL outputs"] L --> O O --> P["PreviewImage or Diagram Viewer URL"] This is a conceptual view of the documented nodes, not a requirement to use an LLM.
2. What the code does with model output nodes/uml_diagram.py[1] normalizes strings and several response shapes, extracts fenced diagram blocks, and prefers a block matching the selected type. That helps when a model returns prose around Mermaid code.
Extraction is not the same thing as syntax validation. A clean code block can still contain a broken diagram; the renderer must accept it.
3. From rendered bytes to a ComfyUI image Raster output is opened with Pillow, converted to RGB, normalized to floating-point values between zero and one, and wrapped as a tensor shaped [1, H, W, 3].
SVG is different. The code attempts a CairoSVG conversion for an image preview. For non-raster output without a successful conversion, it can return a tiny placeholder tensor while preserving the file output. That distinction explains why a saved SVG and its preview may behave differently.
4. Start with the smallest workflow comfy node install comfyui-uml Then restart ComfyUI and try the repository’s uml_single_diagram_only.json: UMLDiagram → PreviewImage. Add the viewer after rendering works. The repository also supplies Mermaid, PlantUML, and Ollama examples.
The web backend sends diagram source to the selected Kroki service. For sensitive architecture or offline use, the repository documents optional local Mermaid and Graphviz paths. Local Mermaid needs its JavaScript dependencies; SVG preview may need CairoSVG.
5. Source trail README, screenshot and installation[2] Rendering node implementation[1] Example workflows[3] The MCP diagram project
summary: How ComfyUI-UML turns Mermaid and PlantUML source into images, file outputs and viewer links, with Kroki and optional local renderers.

AlgoETS/BatchBacktesting ★ 3 · 4 forks · Repository created 2023-03-29
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. A batch backtest is a small data pipeline: choose instruments, obtain prices, clean the observations, run a strategy, and save comparable results. AlgoETS/BatchBacktesting makes those steps visible in Python rather than hiding them behind a dashboard.
This image is an existing article illustration, not a new benchmark run.
1. Follow a single instrument first In src/BatchBacktesting.py[1], process_instrument selects a stock or crypto price adapter, cleans the data, and constructs a Backtest. It attaches the instrument and strategy names to the result before returning it.
flowchart TD I["Instrument list and strategy"] --> P["ThreadPoolExecutor"] P --> D["Fetch and clean historical data"] D --> B["Backtest per instrument"] B --> R["Result with Instrument and Strategy"] R --> C["Per-instrument CSV"] R --> A["Aggregate strategy CSV"] B --> H["Optional HTML chart"] The single-strategy runner defaults to four workers. Plot generation is optional. Those are code defaults, not measured throughput.
2. The assumptions are in the constructor The inspected runner uses 100,000 starting cash, 0.002 commission (0.2%), and exclusive orders. These settings belong beside any comparison of returns.
They still do not cover every market cost or data issue. Slippage, availability of short positions, delisted securities, and corporate actions need separate review.
3. An EMA detail worth noticing strategies.py[2] computes 20-, 80-, and 150-period EMAs for the EMA class. Its entry decisions compare the 20 and 80 curves; the 150-period curve is calculated but not used in those next conditions.
The long-side rule closes the prior position and buys with a stop at 90% of the current price and a target at 125%. This is the implemented experiment, not a claim that those parameters are optimal.
4. Keep comparable rows together The runner writes per-instrument CSVs, an aggregate CSV per strategy, and optional HTML charts. The README links a published AAPL EMA chart covering 2018-04-04 through 2023-04-03. Those are that example’s dates, not a fixed range for every run.
Open the published AAPL example[3].
One analysis trap appears in analyse.py[4]: groupby("Instrument").max() takes each column’s maximum independently. The resulting row can combine metrics from different runs. Select a real row by return before narrating its drawdown and duration.
5. Know the failure boundaries A failed instrument returns None. If all instruments fail, the later concatenation has no frames. The multi-strategy helper also creates an outer pool around inner pools, so API rate limits and nested concurrency deserve attention.
These are observations from reading the source. I did not rerun financial simulations for this article or generate new return claims.
6. Sources and related posts Repository and historical example[5] Runner implementation[1] Strategies[2] Analysis helpers[4] Earlier multi-ticker article
summary: Reading BatchBacktesting’s Python engine: worker pools, 0.2% commission, strategy defaults, CSV outputs and pitfalls in aggregate analysis.
title: Inside BatchBacktesting: parallel runs, explicit assumptions and useful outputs

antoinebou12/sm64coopdx-switch-N3DS ★ 4 · 1 forks · Repository created 2026-08-19
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-11-05. The interesting part of a console port is rarely a single compiler flag. sm64coopdx-switch-N3DS brings the Coop Deluxe engine to two very different handheld targets. The work lives at the platform boundary: graphics, input, audio, threading, and packaging.
This fork builds on the Coop Deluxe Team’s sm64coopdx, which continues djoslin0’s sm64ex-coop. The multiplayer engine and Lua ecosystem are upstream work; the console adapters are the focus here.
1. One engine, different platform services flowchart TD E["Shared CoopDX engine and Lua mods"] --> A["Platform APIs"] A --> S["Switch target"] A --> N["New 3DS target"] S --> SI["Switch controller backend"] S --> SN["Switch packaging and networking"] N --> G["Citro3D / PICA200 renderer"] N --> I["Circle Pad, C-Stick and touch"] N --> AU["NDSP audio and libctru threads"] The repository’s New 3DS port notes[1] explicitly require that desktop and Switch builds gain no libctru, Citro3D, or devkitARM dependencies from the new target. That is the architectural constraint worth preserving.
2. New 3DS is a graphics translation problem The New 3DS backend implements CoopDX’s rendering API through Citro3D and PICA200. It translates common color-combiner paths into TEV stages, handles texture swizzling, depth, scissor, blending, and fog, and reports degraded combiner cases.
That last point matters. A backend that compiles is not automatically a faithful renderer. Explicit diagnostics tell you where the target GPU cannot represent an effect in the initial implementation.
The hardware foundation also separates the 400×240 top screen from the 320×240 bottom screen. Native controls map Circle Pad movement and C-Stick camera input. NDSP uses bounded buffers for stereo PCM16 audio.
3. Build the shell before the game There are two New 3DS paths: a small platform shell in Makefile.new3ds, and full-game integration in Makefile.new3ds-game.
make -f Makefile.new3ds port-smoke -j2 make -f Makefile.new3ds-game new3ds-integration-smoke -j2 These are documented compile checks, not commands I ran as part of writing this article. Separate Docker compose files and build subtrees keep the Switch and New 3DS toolchains apart.
4. Release files do not settle hardware status The README links a New 3DS release, while the detailed port notes still say not to call the port playable and describe hardware gameplay as unverified. Those signals should be read together: an artifact exists, but that alone does not establish stability or full multiplayer compatibility.
Switch documentation covers CoopNet, local wireless, an in-game keypad, crash diagnostics, and packaging. Consult the Switch installation guide[2] for current instructions.
Builds require your own legally obtained North American SM64 ROM. This article supplies no ROM or extracted game assets.
5. Source trail Repository and README[3] New 3DS architecture and verification status[1] Switch build notes[4] Switch controller adapter[5]

antoinebou12/Serilog.Sinks.SentrySDK ★ 2 · 0 forks · Repository created 2023-06-05
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. A log line tells you that something happened. An error event becomes useful when it also carries the exception, release, environment, and request context needed to investigate it. Serilog.Sinks.SentrySDK connects those two views.
This project is based on serilog-contrib/serilog-sinks-sentry. Its own GitHub stars measure interest in this repository, not total Serilog or Sentry adoption.
1. The adapter boundary flowchart TD A["Application"] --> L["Serilog LogEvent"] L --> S["SentrySink"] S --> W["ISentrySdkWrapper"] W --> SDK["Sentry .NET SDK"] SDK --> E["Sentry event reporting"] C["ASP.NET Core context middleware"] -. context .-> S SentrySink.cs[1] implements ILogEventSink and IDisposable. An ISentrySdkWrapper abstracts message capture, exception capture, and transaction creation. That boundary also makes SDK interactions replaceable in tests.
2. Initialize once The sink configures Sentry internally. Its constructor rejects an empty DSN, prepares options, and owns an initialization handle. The README warns against adding a second independent SentrySdk.Init in the same process.
This is easy to miss in a web application that already initializes monitoring elsewhere. Decide who owns initialization before adding the sink.
dotnet add package Serilog.Sinks.SentrySDK The repository includes console and ASP.NET Core demos. Use their configuration examples for the installed version rather than copying an arbitrary overload from an older package.
3. Context needs deliberate handling The companion ASP.NET Core project contains a request adapter, destructuring policy, exception extensions, and context middleware. Request context helps diagnose failures, but it should be selected deliberately. Review PII settings and filtering before sending application data.
The sink exposes advanced options and a beforeSend callback. Its code documents callback ordering around EventId mapping; that is useful when filtering or enriching events without overwriting the sink’s own mapping.
4. Packages and adoption The current README describes two main package IDs that target net6.0 and net10.0, plus separate .6 and .10 variants. This describes package targets, not a recommendation about runtime support lifecycles.
[4]
The badge is a live download count for that package ID. It excludes the separately published variants, and downloads are not the same as active installations. The dated repository snapshot above is kept separate.
5. What the checks establish The README documents xUnit tests, coverage collection, and formatting checks. CI and release badges are linked evidence; this article does not claim those checks were rerun here or invent a coverage percentage.
6. Sources README and package matrix[2] Sink implementation[1] Console and web demos[3] NuGet package statistics[4]

AlgoETS/Workshop1 ★ 3 · 0 forks · Repository created 2023-09-07
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. The most useful beginner workshop gives each new concept somewhere to go. AlgoETS/Workshop1 moves from Python setup to an API response, a DataFrame, and a chart. The final notebook uses Apple price data and exponential moving averages to bring those steps together.
1. Nine notebooks, six stages The repository contains nine Jupyter notebooks across six numbered directories: two setup notebooks, two Python notebooks, one API notebook, one pandas notebook, two visualization notebooks, and one final project.
This is a count of checked-in teaching material, not a student attendance or completion statistic.
flowchart TD S["Environment and cloud notebooks"] --> P["Python basics and advanced concepts"] P --> A["Read API responses"] A --> D["Clean and explore with pandas"] D --> V["Visualize the data"] V --> E["Apple prices and EMA project"] 2. Keep setup from swallowing the lesson The README links a Colab entry point[1]. Local Jupyter is also documented. Offering both lets learners begin with code while keeping environment setup available as its own topic.
The six-stage structure makes it possible to return to a missing concept without restarting the entire project.
3. The final exercise is concrete The code in 5.1_project_ema.ipynb[2] plots Apple closing prices with 12-, 26-, 50-, 100-, and 200-day EMA curves. This is a more precise description than the README’s broad “advanced exploration and modeling” language.
The exercise connects a request, tabular data, indicator columns, and a labeled chart. It does not establish that any crossover makes money.
4. Read the chart as a data exercise Useful classroom questions are technical: are dates ordered correctly? Were missing values removed intentionally? Why does a longer EMA respond more slowly? Are all curves computed from the same observations?
API availability, keys, and package versions can change since the original workshop. The notebooks are teaching material to inspect and adapt, not a promise of a fresh one-command environment.
5. From one chart to a batch experiment The natural continuation is BatchBacktesting: the same indicator idea, now evaluated across instruments with recorded assumptions and comparable outputs.
That progression keeps the focus on understanding data and code before interpreting a leaderboard.
6. Sources Workshop repository and original artwork[3] Python basics notebook[4] EMA project code[2]

Three repos I maintain on the side: Artemis-Switch[1] for Apollo/Sunshine streaming on Switch, moonlight-N3DS[2] for GameStream on New 3DS, and sm64coopdx-switch[3] as a Switch build of cooperative Super Mario 64. They share the same itch — run something interesting on hardware that was not designed for it — but the stack and constraints differ.
1. Artemis-Switch — PC streaming on Switch Artemis-Switch[1] is my fork of XITRIX/Moonlight-Switch[4], wired for Apollo (Sunshine) hosts instead of classic NVIDIA GameStream. I stream Steam Big Picture from my desktop (AntoinePC) and use the in-app overlay for quick host shortcuts and a live performance panel.
The Quick tab exposes window-management shortcuts (Win+Shift+Left / Right), keyboard presets, and Apollo host scripts without leaving the stream. Handy when the host is a Windows box and the Switch is just the display.
Performance shows bitrate (~12 Mbps in this capture), Switch Wi-Fi bars, and receive / decode / render timings. Render is usually the bottleneck on Switch; sub-millisecond receive and decode means the network and decoder are healthy and the frame budget is mostly compositing.
Repo: github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-Switch[1] (★ 12). Upstream Moonlight-Switch work also shows up on my CV as merged toolchain fixes[4] for newer devkitPro toolchains — separate from the Artemis fork, same Moonlight lineage.
2. moonlight-N3DS — GameStream on New 3DS moonlight-N3DS[2] tracks zoeyjodon/moonlight-N3DS[5], a GameStream client for New 3DS (extra RAM and CPU vs OG 3DS). My fork is where I experiment with build fixes and integration; star count on my repo is still low — the community interest lives on upstream (~300★), which is the right place to look for installs and issues.
Constraints are brutal: 400×240 top screen, software decode, Wi-Fi on a 2015 handheld. Expect lower bitrate and higher latency than Switch; the win is having any Moonlight path on 3DS at all.
Repo: github.com/antoinebou12/moonlight-N3DS[2].
3. sm64coopdx-switch — co-op Mario 64 on Switch sm64coopdx-switch[3] ports coop-deluxe/sm64coopdx[6] to Switch homebrew. sm64coopdx is the continuation of sm64ex-coop: online co-op, Lua mods, and QoL the decomp scene added over years.
Legal note: like every SM64 port, you must supply your own legally obtained ROM. The repo builds the port; it does not ship game assets.
Repo: github.com/antoinebou12/sm64coopdx-switch[3].

content:
Couplage contact-apparence pour l’usure de surfaces microstructurées en simulation interactive — my ÉTS master’s thesis (English abstract title: Visual Appearance Evolution from Wear on Microstructured Surfaces in Texture Space). Directed by Sheldon Andrews, defended 14 August 2026. The core idea: give material maps a persistent local memory of contact. Body travel alone cannot predict where wear shows up.
1. The gap Real surfaces keep a trace of friction and slip. Interactive simulators usually throw that away at the end of each timestep. The contact solver already computes impulses, relative velocity, tangential traction, and dissipation — then updates rigid-body motion and stops. Material maps (albedo, roughness, normals) stay fixed unless an artist paints wear by hand.
The thesis closes that loop: mechanical contact resolution feeds texture-space appearance evolution at the places contact actually happened.
2. Pipeline (one glance) Sparse contacts are grouped into local patches, projected into material atlases, and reconstructed as tangential velocity, effective traction, and frictional dissipation on a GPU patch grid. Those fields drive accumulation of sliding distance, dominant direction, and wear — then progressive map updates without global remeshing.
Source: wear-pipeline-flow.mmd (same chain as GraphQuon 2025). The interactive implementation in TextureFriction adds a stricter runtime order: pre-solve FBO passes → PGS or AVBD solve → post-solve velocity/traction → sliding/wear/direction deposit → rendering.
3. Three contributions Dissipation-based local accumulation — links sliding, reconstructed traction, and visual surface evolution in texture space. Contact-to-atlas projection architecture — patch clustering, GPU buffers, persistent material memory on a fixed mesh; sliding, direction, and wear written where overlap says contact occurred. GelSight acquisition and comparison — controlled wear bench captures build the Wear Surface Texture Datasets and calibrate simulated patterns against measured microgeometry. 4. Two codebases Repo Role WearPaper (not public) LaTeX thesis sources, ACM article, Beamer defense slides, and canonical bibliography. TextureFriction (local, E:\master\TextureFriction) Qt6 + OpenGL 4.3+ simulator: PGS/AVBD contact, cluster FBO passes, GPU deposition into sliding/wear/direction atlases. Build: just build, run: just run-build. See docs/architecture/14-thesis-pipeline-and-rationale.md in the repo. WearPaper is the paper trail; TextureFriction is where the loop runs at interactive rates.
5. Validation Acquisitions on a reciprocal abrasion bench feed measured normal maps and staged wear progression. Public dataset: ETSim/WearSurfacesDatasets[1]. Surface metrology tooling connects to my CV work on TrueMapData[2] and surfalize integration.
6. Results (snapshot) In tested scenarios, written texels track cumulative wear more closely than body travel alone; contact topology changes the deposit pattern. A cube or torus on a plane stays within an interactive budget; cost rises sharply when several contact groups are processed together. The method is a physically motivated appearance model, not a full tribology simulator — limits remain around effective-field reconstruction, calibration, and UV parameterization.
7. Research materials The manuscript sources, article, and defense slides live in WearPaper, which is not public.
8. Related GraphQuon 2025 — Where to Wear? — conference talk on the same research line Software engineering journey — ÉTS master’s thread (rendering, physics, wear) CV education line: Thesis: real-time surface wear in interactive physics simulations, with dynamic friction and textures
summary: ÉTS master's thesis on real-time surface wear in interactive simulation — frictional dissipation, GPU texture atlases, GelSight validation, WearPaper and TextureFriction.

title: Master's thesis — contact–appearance coupling for wear in texture space

7. Step 5 — Resin print Resin for small parts. Tilt overhangs toward the plate; light supports on hair and capes.
Check floating islands with the slicer or UVtools[1] before printing.

I taught a thread on “find movies like this” that kept growing: embeddings in PostgreSQL, the same idea in Qdrant with two different vector meanings, then retrieval + a local LLM grounded on the same rows. This page is the story; notebooks and animations live in AlgoETS/SimilityVectorEmbedding[1].
AlgoETS/SimilityVectorEmbedding ★ 1 · 0 forks · Repository created 2024-05-06
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. 1. The original demos These three animations come from the project README. They show recorded interfaces and processing steps, not current latency measurements.
Gradio interface: exploring similar movies.
Still from the Gradio UI — single-title search.
Generating vector representations with Sentence Transformers.
t-SNE of movie embeddings — cluster structure in 2D.
The Qdrant search and recommendation workflow.
Graph view: Superman neighborhood, genres, and cast centrality.
2. What the notebooks actually build postgres/1.create_table.ipynb[2] combines title, year, genres, actors, director, summary, and country into model input. It compares five model configurations: BART, GTE, MiniLM-L12, RoBERTa, and e5-large. This is a code inventory, not an accuracy ranking.
qdrant/0.simple.ipynb[3] creates a 384-dimensional collection with cosine distance and upserts batches of 100 points. The dimension must match the selected encoder. The notebook recreates its collection, so inspect that step before using an existing database.
flowchart TD J["movies.json metadata"] --> T["Combined and preprocessed text"] T --> E["Selected encoder"] E --> N["Normalize vectors"] N --> P["PostgreSQL / pgvector"] N --> Q["Qdrant vector collection"] R["Query encoded with the same model"] --> P R --> Q P --> K["Nearest movies"] Q --> K K --> G["Interface and explanation"] This editable Mermaid replaces a static architecture screenshot. It summarizes the shared dense-vector path without pretending different encoders share one interchangeable vector space.
3. The question behind all three parts Recommendation systems usually hide three different questions:
Plot language — “films that feel like this description.” Taste overlap — “users who rated like you.” Explainability — “why these titles?” with text the user asked. Parts 1–3 map to those questions. Mixing them without labeling the vector type is how demos lie.
4. Part 1 — PostgreSQL, pgvector, and honest SQL 4.1. Build the catalog Start from structured movie JSON (movies.json[4] in the course repo). Concatenate title, year, genres, cast, summary; encode with Sentence Transformers (MiniLM, GTE, etc.); store typed vector columns beside relational fields.
Why pgvector? Vectors stay next to SQL you already trust. Distance operators (<=> cosine, <-> L2) turn kNN into ORDER BY … LIMIT.
SELECT title, 1 - (embedding_minilm <=> ( SELECT embedding_minilm FROM movies WHERE title = $1 )) AS similarity FROM movies WHERE title IS DISTINCT FROM $1 ORDER BY similarity DESC LIMIT 10; Swap column names per model — the course keeps several embedding_* columns to compare neighborhoods side by side.
4.2. What students learn here Normalizing embeddings for cosine. How choice of encoder shifts “similar” (BART vs MiniLM vs e5-large). That SQL transparency beats a black-box API when you are debugging wrong neighbors. Full plots and distribution charts: Medium Part 1[5] and postgres/ notebooks in the repo.
5. Part 2 — Qdrant, MovieLens, dense vs sparse Same “similarity in vector space,” different semantics:
Collection Vector type Question it answers Movies Dense text embedding “Like this wording / vibe” Users (profile) Dense User representation in same space (seed pipeline) Ratings Sparse movieId → rating “Users with overlapping taste” Dense path: encode query text with MiniLM, search movies collection — mirrors Part 1 but in Qdrant’s API.
Sparse path: build NamedSparseVector from a user’s ratings, find similar users, aggregate their high scores on unseen movies — collaborative filtering without training a neural net in the notebook.
FastAPI teaching project (movie_recommendation in the course repo) exposes both flows to a simple HTML UI.
Starter notebook: qdrant/0.simple.ipynb before MovieLens scale.
6. Part 3 — RAG with LangChain + Ollama Reuse pgvector rows as evidence:
flowchart LR Q[User question] --> E[Embed question] E --> SQL[kNN in SQL] SQL --> Rows[Top movies] Rows --> LLM[Ollama via LangChain] LLM --> A[Grounded answer] Pipeline: HuggingFaceEmbeddings → SQL ordering by <=> on embedding_MiniLM → prompt that includes schema + retrieved rows → Ollama(model="llama2:13b-chat").
The saved notebook output is instructive because it fails politely:
LangChain warns on unknown vector column types. The LLM sometimes emits SQL that is not valid pgvector. Heavy models timeout under load. RAG is not “embed and forget” — you need validation, smaller models, or hybrid retrieval.
Notebook: postgres/3.LLMS.ipynb.
7. When not to use this stack Situation Better path Cold-start users with no ratings Dense metadata only Billion-scale sparse CF Specialized CF stack, not demo Qdrant Sub-10 ms latency at huge QPS Managed vector DB + tuning Legal need for exact quotes RAG + citation checks, not raw LLM 8. Takeaway Embed → store → nearest neighbors three times, with three meanings of “neighbor.” Part 3 teaches humility: generators drift from executable SQL unless you constrain them.
9. Related posts Snowflake Data-for-Breakfast — warehouse storytelling Experimentation with technical indicators — another AlgoETS thread 10. References AlgoETS/SimilityVectorEmbedding[1] Medium — Part 1[5] pgvector[6] · Qdrant docs[7] Originally published on Medium[5]; this page merges Parts 1–3.
summary: A teaching narrative: pgvector kNN in SQL, Qdrant dense and sparse vectors on MovieLens, then LangChain + Ollama RAG on the same catalog.

content:
I took part in QcES (Spring 2024 cohort) while working through lean discovery: business model canvas, customer interviews, short pitches, and everything in between. This post is my own recap—not an official program document. Full article in French if you prefer.
1. What stuck with me The program kept coming back to a few ideas. The Business Model Canvas is a shared map for how you create, deliver, and capture value—and whether the idea is desirable, feasible, and viable. You usually start with who you serve and what you promise them, then revise as the market talks back.
Segmentation sounds dry until you try pitching to “doctors” or “parents.” Splitting B2B (firmographics) from B2C (demographics, behavior) makes the market something you can actually reach.
Interviews are for learning, not closing a sale. The facilitators repeated it until it landed: connect, don’t convince; stay curious about the problem, not married to your first solution.
Short feedback rounds (one real strength, one growth angle) and a ~90 second pitch without slides force clarity early. A roadmap is a strategic view over time—not a Gantt chart. And PoC, prototype, and MVP are different beats: can it work, how do people interact, what is the smallest thing you can put in front of real users.
For pitching, Hook → Believe → Join showed up again and again: problem first, then why you’re credible, then a specific ask.
2. How the pieces connect You do not fill the canvas once and frame it. You state a hypothesis, talk to people, adjust segments and value proposition, decide what belongs on a roadmap, then practice explaining it out loud.
flowchart LR hyp[Hypothesis] --> int[Interview] int --> ins[Insight] ins --> bmc[BMC and segment] bmc --> road[Roadmap] road --> pit[Pitch] 3. Business model canvas Nine blocks, one page: segments, value proposition, channels, relationships, revenue, resources, activities, partners, costs. The point is not decoration—it is survival. Every block can break you if you ignore it, and the canvas should move when customers or competitors shift.
We were pushed to nail for whom and how you help before optimizing the rest. That matches the hypothesis–validation loop: test beliefs about the customer and the problem, not only the tech stack.
4. Customer segments Who pays is not always who uses. An early customer often has a real problem, knows it, is looking for options, maybe already hacked a workaround, and might have budget.
B2B segments lean on company size, sector, and buying dynamics. B2C adds lifestyle and behavior. The win is replacing vague labels with groups you can find, email, and interview.
5. Sharing the idea Ninety seconds, no deck: state the problem in plain language, who benefits, what you offer, and why it matters. You are not expected to quote TAM on day one—it is a clarity filter.
When you receive feedback, listen to understand. When you give it, name something that works, then one concrete “what would make this stronger.”
6. Interviews This was the heart of the cohort for me. Interviews fill the gaps a first canvas always has. Do not pitch your fix on the call—learn how the other person lives the problem.
Talk to people beyond the “ideal customer”: users of substitutes, experts, suppliers, communities. Discovery does not end after three calls; it continues through pivots.
Finding people, booking time, and running a useful conversation are skills. The line I still repeat: fall in love with the problem, not the solution.
7. Roadmap, PoC, prototype, MVP A roadmap answers where you are headed for a given audience (team, investors, partners) over a chosen horizon. It is not the same as a detailed project plan.
Proof of concept checks whether the approach can work. A prototype explores interaction—often before a real launch. An MVP is the smallest version you put in front of real users to learn fast, including from what breaks.
Roadmaps look different in discovery, validation, and growth. That alone saved me from over-planning too early.
8. Market and value proposition Market work is more than counting accounts. Macro forces, industry dynamics, customer behavior, and trends set constraints and openings.
Value proposition is offer plus customer benefit—what you deliver and why someone cares. Pain points and “why now” become interview questions, not slide filler.
9. Pitching: Hook, Believe, Join A pitch asks for a next step: time, intros, lab access, funding. Formats vary; structure helps.
Hook — the problem and why it matters to a real audience. Do not open with the product. Believe — the solution, differentiation, evidence (traction, team, recent wins). Join — a specific ask: money, expertise, partnership, introduction. A simple ~90 second scaffold: who you are, problem, offer for a target, value proposition, contrast with alternatives, recent milestone, call to action.
10. What I would tell a founder friend Stage Do this Skip this Week 1 Write who hurts and how you will find them Logo and LLC debate Week 2–3 Five interviews, same script Pitching strangers your solution Week 4 Update BMC once with evidence Fake revenue line in slides Before demo day 90 s pitch aloud daily Adding a fifteenth feature 11. Related posts Professional résumé + JSON Resume — packaging the same story for hiring MarketWatch Python library — side project born from AlgoÉTS energy 12. Closing QcES tied tools to habits: canvas, segmentation, roadmap on one side; interviews, feedback, pitching on the other. The thread is keeping the problem central, making assumptions testable, and speaking clearly enough that people can help—not just nod.
If you are in a similar program, a few well-run interviews usually teach more than a perfectly styled canvas. Consistency beats polish.
summary: Notes from the QcES entrepreneurship program — business canvas, customer interviews, feedback, roadmap, and pitching without drowning in jargon.

I wanted to automate chores in MarketWatch’s virtual stock game (paper trading, not a real broker). marketwatch[1] on PyPI is the small client I shipped — watchlists, game state, portfolio, orders, leaderboard.
1. Why build this Course and side projects already used BatchBacktesting on historical data — see experimentation with indicators. MarketWatch’s game is a different beast: session cookies, game rules, and leaderboards that change with the semester. A thin Python wrapper beat curl scripts in a notebook.
I also wanted a documented surface for teammates: “here is how you list games” beats sharing a gist that rots when the HTML form changes. The package is intentionally small — no ORM, no strategy engine — just HTTP shaped like the site.
2. Design choices Choice Reason Class-based client One login, many calls in a script Explicit methods per endpoint Easier to grep when MarketWatch changes a path Docs on GitHub Pages PyPI description alone is too short for auth edge cases No bundled strategies Keeps the library neutral; strategies belong in your repo 3. Links Package: pypi.org/project/marketwatch[1] Documentation: antoinebou12.github.io/marketwatch[2] Source & issues: github.com/antoinebou12/marketwatch[3] 4. What it can do Area Methods (see docs for signatures) Watchlists Create, list, update symbols Games List games, read settings Portfolio Positions, pending orders Trading Buy / sell inside game rules Social Leaderboard for a game Useful for small bots and screening inside the game — not HFT, not brokerage.
5. Quick start pip install marketwatch from marketwatch import MarketWatch mw = MarketWatch("your_username", "your_password") mw.get_games() mw.get_price("AAPL") Login edge cases (2FA absent, session expiry) are documented on the site — read before cron-scheduling anything.
6. Limits and responsibility Unofficial API — HTML/JSON endpoints can change; pin versions and expect breakage. Terms of use — automation may conflict with MarketWatch rules; use for learning, not abuse. Not financial advice — paper gains do not validate a strategy; pair with honest backtests on separate data. For research-style batch runs on many tickers, see multiple indicators backtesting and Monte Carlo risk bands.
7. Related posts Experimentation with technical indicators Economics of LEGO with data science — another “Python for curiosity” project Questions or bugs: GitHub issues[3].

GraphQuon is the annual Quebec–Ontario pre-SIGGRAPH workshop. The 2025 edition ran 15–16 November 2025 at the University of Toronto (series page[1]). I presented there with Sheldon Andrews (ÉTS): Where to Wear? — how frictional contact leaves a readable history on surfaces, and how we can turn that into graphics and engineering feedback.
1. What I presented Talk title: Where to Wear? (subtitle on the opening slide: Every surface has a biography written by frictional contact).
The story is simple to state and hard to simulate: time, contact, and energy dissipation change how a surface looks and behaves—from bathroom tile wear patterns at an engineering school to scratches on tools, gaming materials, and robotics grippers. The deck walks from motivation through mechanics (Archard wear, energy-based wear laws), a graphics-oriented pipeline (contact mask, orthographic volumes, tangential velocity and traction, texture integration), and validation ideas (GelSight capture, materials atlas interpolation).

After helping with the GraphQuon 2024 site at ÉTS, presenting in Toronto in 2025 felt like the same community on the other side of the drive.
The research line connects to my ÉTS work on 3D fabrication and validation of frictional surfaces (project description[2]).

content:
Blender add-ons that need NumPy, meshio, or requests hit the same wall: Blender ships its own Python, so system pip does nothing useful. I wrote a small installer that targets Blender’s sys.executable, drops wheels under scripts/modules, and runs in a background thread so the UI stays responsive (Blender 4.2+, Windows).
1. The problem in one sentence You cannot pip install globally and expect import meshio inside Blender — the interpreter path is Blender’s bundled runtime.
2. Strategy Piece Role sys.executable Invoke pip against Blender’s Python bpy.utils.user_resource("SCRIPTS", path="modules") Writable install dir per user/version site.addsitedir Make imports resolve next launch Background thread + bpy.app.timers Avoid freezing the UI; show popups when done 3. The installer script (core idea) REQUIRED_PACKAGES = { "fileseq": "fileseq==1.15.2", "meshio": "meshio==5.3.4", "rich": "rich==13.7.0", "requests": "requests==2.31.0", } def install_package(package, modules_path): subprocess.check_call([ sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--upgrade", "--target", modules_path, package, ]) Full script in the Medium article[1] and my repo copies — includes progress bar hooks and __import__ checks to skip already-installed wheels.
4. How to run it Option A — Scripting workspace: paste in Text Editor → Run Script → wait for popup.
Option B — Add-on register():
def register(): modules_path = get_modules_path() append_modules_to_sys_path(modules_path) background_install_packages(REQUIRED_PACKAGES, modules_path) Ship dependencies with your add-on so users are not guessing which Python to use.
5. Troubleshooting Restart Blender after first install. print(sys.path) if imports fail — confirm modules is listed. Version pin wheels — Blender’s Python version is not your system 3.12. 6. When not to use this pattern Case Why Add-on targets many Blender versions Pin and test per minor version Heavy CUDA stacks May exceed user GPU/driver setup Corporate locked-down PCs pip may be blocked — vendor wheels manually 7. Takeaway Automate dependency install inside Blender’s sandbox; users stop emailing “which Python?” — you own the matrix in REQUIRED_PACKAGES.
8. Related posts Skate rack — CAD to plywood — physical maker pipeline AI figurines / 3D print — mesh tools in another ecosystem 9. References Blender API[2] Managing Python in Blender[3] Python packaging guide[4] Originally published on Medium[1].
summary: Install pip packages into Blender’s embedded Python — user modules folder, background thread, popups — without breaking the core install.
title: A Method to Install Python Packages for Add-ons & Plugins in Blender (Windows, Blender 4.2+)

GraphQuon (formerly MOTOGRAPH) is the annual Quebec–Ontario pre-SIGGRAPH workshop for East-Canadian computer graphics labs. The 2024 edition ran 9–10 November 2024 at École de technologie supérieure (ÉTS) in Montréal. I helped build and host the conference website at graphquon.github.io[1] so schedules, registration, and past editions stayed in one place.
1. What GraphQuon is for From the site’s About the event copy: students present prospective SIGGRAPH-bound work to a friendly, constructively critical audience and get feedback before the real submission crunch. Faculty groups across Quebec and Ontario rotate hosting; 2024 was ÉTS’s turn.
Questions for organizers: graphquon@etsmtl.ca.
1.1. Earlier names Year Name Dates 2018 MOTOGRAPH Nov 17–18 2019 MOTOGRAPH Dec 7–8 2021 Tomatograph Dec 3–4 2022 FOIEGRAPH Nov 11–12 2023 GRAPHQUON Dec 2–3 2024 GRAPHQUON Nov 9–10 @ ÉTS 2. 2024 schedule (highlights) Full timetables live on graphquon.github.io[1]. A few anchors I remember from the published program:
Saturday 9 November
Morning talks included Quoc-Minh Ton-That, Melissa Katz (McGill), and Ivan Puhachov (UdeM) among the honourable mentions. Midday ÉTS/Sherbrooke block: Justin Benoist, Arthur Delon, Joel Pelletier-Guenette. Afternoon: Abhishek Madan (Toronto); Clara Kim (Waterloo) won Best presentation. Sunday 10 November
Morning honourable mentions included Victor Rong, Ryusuke Sugimoto, Yue Chang, and Ege Ciklabakkal. Late afternoon ÉTS/MILA block: Alex Hoang-Cao, Darsh Kaushik. The room itself matched the workshop vibe: ÉTS auditorium, red carpet, simple stage, and a lot of white chairs filled between sessions.
3. Hallway highlight: Masha Shugrina (NVIDIA) Between sessions I talked with Masha Shugrina (NVIDIA Spatial Intelligence Lab / creative AI tools). Two demos stuck with me:
Diffusion Texture Painting[2] (SIGGRAPH 2024) — painting on UV-mapped meshes with a diffusion brush so strokes stay seamless and you can blend complex reference textures interactively, not just stamp pixels. A Gaussian-splat style environment scan — a simple scene you could walk around in, the kind of collider/scan setup that makes spatial content feel immediate without a heavy offline pipeline. (NVIDIA’s newer line of work includes Gaussian splat painting[3] research; the booth conversation was about that direction more than a single paper title.) It was the useful kind of industry chat: concrete tools you could imagine plugging into a lab pipeline, not a slide deck of buzzwords.
4. Audience and vibe Mostly graphics + vision grad students and faculty from Quebec and Ontario — people who understand meshes and shaders but still want a friendly room. Talks skewed research-heavy; questions were about evaluation protocols and whether a method would survive a SIGGRAPH reviewer, not startup pitch decks.
5. My role vs 2025 For 2024 I was on the organizing/web side (site on GitHub Pages, schedule pages, contact blocks). That meant I learned the boring critical path: bios on time, PDF links that do not 404, and a schedule page that works on mobile in a hallway. In 2025 I presented at the Toronto edition — see GraphQuon 2025 — University of Toronto (Where to Wear? with Sheldon Andrews). Organizing first made presenting calmer — I already knew where the HDMI adapter lived.
6. Tips if you attend next year Bring a question for the presenters — honourable mentions get sharp feedback when they name what they want (SIGGRAPH track, clarity, eval). Talk in the hall — half the value is comparing pipelines with other Quebec/Ontario labs. Check the site early — schedules shift; graphquon.github.io[1] is the source of truth. 7.
