Snowflake Data-for-Breakfast was a morning conference on the cloud data platform — warehousing, sharing, governance, and customer stories that make abstract architecture feel operational. I went to hear how teams actually run Snowflake, not to collect swag. Infostrux ran a keynote that tied the room together.
1. Why I attended I was touching data platforms on coursework and side projects — enough SQL to be dangerous, not enough production war stories. A breakfast format is low commitment: if the first talk is weak, you still leave before lunch with one useful vocabulary word (clean room, share, row access policy).
2. Overview materials The opening deck framed Snowflake as governed sharing first, raw speed second. That ordering matters when your org’s fear is “we cannot expose that table,” not “we need another cluster.”
3. What stuck from customer stories 3.1. Global healthcare operations One healthcare customer ran secure operations across three continents — partner data sharing without losing availability or SLA headroom.
Lesson Detail Replication + governance Compliance is not an afterthought when partners query live Latency budgets Clinical ops cannot wait for overnight batch only Sharing contracts Legal and technical share objects move together That is the pitch for a cloud warehouse when compliance and replication actually work in production — not a slide, a running system.
3.2. Tax-sector analytics at scale Another team needed to land very large datasets and explore them without knowing every question upfront.
Snowflake as a single consolidation and transform layer sped up troubleshooting and made lineage easier to explain to auditors and internal users. The unstated win: analysts stop emailing CSV attachments.
3.3. Data clean rooms Clean rooms came up for due diligence: two companies compare overlapping datasets without dumping everything into one bucket.
Privacy-preserving collaboration is a product story, not only a compliance checkbox — especially for M&A style questions where both sides distrust each other’s IT.
4. Comparison table (my notes) Pattern Good fit Watch out Central warehouse Many teams, shared dimensions Cost without query discipline Data sharing Partners need live slices Contract + row policies Clean room Sensitive overlap analysis Setup time vs one-off export Scale-up compute Exploratory spikes Forgotten warehouses left on 5. Closing Worth the morning if you touch data platforms — good snapshot of where Snowflake pushes (scale, sharing, governed collaboration). I left with clearer vocabulary for customer conversations, even when we are not on Snowflake day to day.
Same conference season as Run:ai on AWS — different stack, same habit of writing notes before the slides fade.
6. Related posts Vector databases and similar movies — another data-heavy thread on the blog Economics of LEGO with data science — playful analytics at home scale

content:
I had boards leaning in every corner, so I designed a vertical rack in CAD, cut angled slots in plywood, and built something that could hold skateboards and a snowboard without drilling into rental walls. December 2021; photos cropped from old stories.
1. Requirements Need Design response 6+ boards Six slots per side panel Snowboard + skates Taller top bay, wider slot mouth Rental-friendly Freestanding lean, no lag bolts Cheap 3/4" plywood, screws, stain 2. Design in CAD Two side panels, three horizontal ties, six downward-angled slots per side so decks slide in and stay put. I modeled in a mainstream mechanical CAD workflow (dimension-driven sketches, assembly check for interference) before buying sheet goods.
Rough intent (not build drawings):
Panel height ~6 ft — snowboard diagonal fit Slot depth ~3/4 deck width — catch without binding on grip Slot angle ~15–20° down — gravity holds board; longboards were tight The CAD render is optimistic — no sawdust, no cat, perfect orthogonality.
3. Metal frame detour (shop class energy) Before the plywood version landed, I welded a tubular orange frame in a school shop — good practice for squareness, honestly overkill for an apartment rack. It never became the final bedroom solution: too heavy, too industrial, and my landlord did not need to know I owned a mini weldment. It still proved the layout — upright posts plus cross-members, slots implied by spacing even before I cut wood.
That prototype was the confidence boost; the rack I actually live with came later from sheet goods, not tube stock.
The photo is pure shop-class energy: fluorescent lights, concrete floor, and a frame that taught me the geometry without surviving the move indoors.
4. Materials — Home Depot run Once the metal idea stayed in the garage, I went to Home Depot for buildable material: one cart of 3/4" plywood (two side panels and shelves), wood screws, stain, and scrap 2×4 for a temporary stand while I dry-fit. No exotic lumber — whatever was flat enough that day.
3/4" plywood — two sides + horizontal ties Wood screws — pre-drill near ends so the ply does not split Stain — brushed on a tarp in a cold December garage 2×4 scrap — propped the frame while slots were still rough 5. Cutting slots Diagonal notch with rounded bottom: spade bit at end, circular saw on straights, file burrs. Clamps, dust, repeat.
6. Assembly and inspection Dry-fit, stain in cold December garage, cat QA on every flat surface.
7. Finished rack Snowboard on top (Union bindings), skates in slots, spare on floor.
8. Next time Steeper slot angle for longboards Edge banding on slot mouths French cleat wall mount when not renting 9. Related posts LiDAR apartment scan with Rhino — measure before you build Home networking lab — another home project thread AI figurines / 3D print — CAD → object years later
summary: Vertical skate rack — shop-class welded frame detour, then Home Depot plywood, CAD slots, and a rental-friendly build, December 2021.
title: Skate rack — from CAD to plywood

content:
I wanted scale readings in Home Assistant next to the rest of my apartment automations — not another siloed health app. That turned into maintaining hass_renpho[1] (a fork of the quiet community integration), running APKLeaks on the Android client, and a Lovelace board I still open when training or sleep changes.
1. Why not only the Renpho app A Renpho scale with bio-impedance spits out more than weight — BMI, BMR, body age, fat and muscle estimates, water, protein, visceral-fat indices, and a pile of resistance fields per limb if you pull the full payload. Useful only if the numbers live where you already look: history graphs, automations, and the same homelab mindset as everything else self-hosted at home.
2. Inspiration (without the cult) Personal tracking, for me, started around the same time people were talking about Bryan Johnson’s “Blueprint” push for self-quantification. I am not selling a protocol — the point was simpler: trends over time, same conditions, don’t panic on one morning spike. The photo below is mood board energy, not medical advice.
3. Where hass_renpho came from Neil Allen’s write-ups — reverse-engineering the Renpho app[2] and Renpho → Home Assistant[3] — did the hard thinking first. The community repo neilzilla/hass-renpho[4] wrapped that into a Home Assistant custom component.
When activity slowed and I needed more entities exposed, I forked to antoinebou12/hass_renpho[1]. The README is honest about constraints:
This integration targets the older Renpho app cloud API. Newer app versions may not work; treat it as a hobby integration, not a supported product.
There is a small API explorer at hass-renpho.vercel.app/docs[5] if you want to poke the JSON with your own credentials before touching HA.
3.1. What the fork actually does Logs into Renpho’s cloud (renpho.qnclouds.com) with email/password (same as the phone app). Polls on a refresh interval you set in YAML or the UI. Exposes sensors for weight, composition, metabolic estimates, device metadata, and optional girth/goals when the account has them. Optional proxy URL when your home IP is throttled or blocked but the app works on cellular data. I kept talking with the original maintainer when it made sense — share payload shapes, avoid duplicate fixes, keep one integration useful for anyone else with a scale in the closet.
4. Install path I used HACS[6] on Home Assistant (or copy custom_components/renpho from the repo). Drop credentials in configuration.yaml (legacy platform style in my fork): renpho: email: you@example.com password: !secret renpho_password refresh: 600 # seconds between polls — logging in here can log you out of the app # proxy: http://127.0.0.1:8080 # optional — only this integration’s traffic sensor: - platform: renpho Restart HA, confirm entities appear, then build Lovelace. Heads-up: polling logs you into the cloud API; Renpho may kick your phone session. I picked a 600s refresh so I was not hammering login on every automation tick.
5. Metrics the integration surfaces The fork documents dozens of fields. In practice I watch a smaller set in Lovelace; the rest are there if you automate or debug.
Group Examples Units Core weight, BMI, body fat, water, muscle, bone kg, % Shape waistline, hip, stature cm Metabolic BMR, protein kcal/day, % Age body age years Visceral / subcutaneous visfat, subfat level, % Device scale name, MAC, model, timezone strings Bio-impedance raw resistance per limb (20 kHz / 100 kHz style fields) ohms Full tables live in the repo README[7] — handy when APKLeaks shows a new key and you need a matching sensor.
6. When the cloud API fights your network Residential or datacenter egress sometimes fails against Renpho’s cloud even when the official app works on LTE. Symptoms: auth errors, empty lists, random HTTP failures in HA logs.
Mitigations from the README:
VPN on the HA host — change egress IP for everything on that machine. proxy in config — only Renpho traffic goes through your HTTP/SOCKS proxy (credentials pass through that path — use something you trust). I document this because it burned an evening that looked like “broken integration” but was really IP reputation.
7. Reverse engineering with APKLeaks Renpho does not ship a public API PDF. Next step: see what the Android APK calls.
APKLeaks[8] scans the package for strings — hosts, paths, keys — without a full decompile session:
pip install apkleaks git clone https://github.com/dwisiswant0/apkleaks cd apkleaks && pip install -r requirements.txt apkleaks -f /path/to/renpho.apk -o renpho-leaks.txt I matched leaked URLs and parameter names to the JSON fields the integration already mapped, then filled gaps when Lovelace showed unknown for a new key after an app update.
Further reading:
APKLeaks on GitHub[8] White Oak Security — APKLeaks overview[9] Treat anything you extract as an unstable contract — store updates break custom integrations; that is the hobby tax.
8. Lovelace dashboards Two views I actually use: vitals + history, then girth/goals when Renpho syncs them.
Weight trend at the top, composition gauges in the middle, “extra” metrics as entities you can hide if they noise you out.
Girth and goals only matter if your Renpho profile has them; otherwise this panel stays empty and that is fine.
9. Context outside HA Renpho is one input. I still mirror activity and food elsewhere (Google Health, MyFitnessPal) so scale readings sit next to movement and calories, not alone in a vacuum.
9.1. Habits that kept the series usable Habit Why Same time of day Mornings, similar hydration — otherwise you are comparing apples to soup Clothing constant ~1 kg swing is normal noise, not “fat overnight” Trends over weeks Bio-impedance composition lags reality; react to slopes Hide gauges you ignore If you do not act on visceral fat %, remove the card This started as a technical side project and became a steady habit: enough signal to notice when training or sleep changes show up in weight and energy, not enough precision for clinic decisions.
10. When not to do this You need clinical body composition — consumer scales estimate, they do not diagnose. You cannot run the legacy app/API path the integration expects. You will not maintain a fork when Renpho changes the app — budget breakage. Daily fat % will ruin your mood — curate the dashboard ruthlessly. 11. Repo links (quick) Resource URL My fork github.com/antoinebou12/hass_renpho[1] Upstream lineage github.com/neilzilla/hass-renpho[4] API docs / playground hass-renpho.vercel.app/docs[5] Original RE blog neilgaryallen.dev — Renpho series[2] 12. Related posts Home networking evolution — same “own your infra” thread MediaBox homelab notes — another self-hosted stack at home Economics of LEGO with data science — another dataset curiosity project If you self-host health data, what actually stuck — Home Assistant, Grafana, or phone-only apps? The gadget is rarely the hard part; fitting the routine is.
summary: Forking hass_renpho for Home Assistant — old Renpho app API, APKLeaks, Lovelace dashboards, proxy quirks, and habits that keep bio-impedance useful.

title: Renpho scale, Home Assistant, and reverse-engineering the API

content:
Cloud bills pushed me toward a home lab: old PCs, Docker instead of SaaS where possible, and enough scripting to rebuild after a bad weekend. This post is how that network grew — not a perfect design, but one that taught routing, VPNs, and virtualization by breaking things locally.
1. Why a home lab University courses covered IP, VPNs, and routing on paper. Running services at home made the tradeoffs real: power, noise, backups, and “who has SSH when the router dies.” I wanted a place to break things without a cloud invoice — and a story I could tell in interviews that was not only “I used AWS once.”
2. Docker first I mapped free container stacks to jobs I was paying for in the cloud — media, dashboards, small utilities. Docker was the on-ramp to treating the homelab as composable services instead of one giant pet server.
Lesson that stuck: one compose file per concern. When Plex misbehaved, I did not rebuild the whole machine — I recycled the volume and learned what actually persisted.
3. Bash and two servers Core hardware: a cheap Dell box plus an older 2004-era machine. Bash scripts for Ubuntu, CentOS, and Proxmox installs — repeatable enough that reinstalling after experiments hurt less.
3.1. Physical rack (October 2022) Before the Lucidchart diagrams, the lab was literally closets and shelves — cable nest included. I cropped these from old story posts; they are the real wiring, not a render.
Wall stack — switch, modem, router, enterprise server (2010-era), and UPS, labeled while I was still learning what plugged into what:
Dell PowerEdge R710 — dual Xeon X5667 (~3 GHz quad-core), 24 GB RAM, running headless beside acoustic foam. The handwritten tape on the bezel was my inventory system:
Closet shelf build — rack server horizontal, yellow switch, monitor for local installs, and enough blue patch cables to teach patience:
Virtualization matters when you snapshot before trying something dumb. A dedicated hypervisor host beat bare-metal churn.
The Lucidchart diagram was the “explain to a roommate” version — which subnet, which box, what is allowed from the internet.
4. Remote access and edge Caddy as reverse proxy; public exposure through an OVH front so home IP is not the only line of defense. Automatic HTTPS mattered more than I expected — fewer manual cert renewals, fewer late-night openssl commands. I later mirrored that habit on AWS; see Caddy + EC2 + CloudWatch.
WireGuard for VPN — annoying to configure the first time, fast once up. I contributed small setup helpers so friends could connect without reading man pages for a week. Split-tunnel vs full-tunnel was the debate every guest had; document your choice on the wiki page you will forget to update.
5. Growth after moving New apartment, more VLAN curiosity, Proxmox VMs for club projects. Lucidchart for the wall diagram; C4-style views when explaining the stack to someone else.
Later I moved public sites toward static hosting (S3/GitHub Pages) to cut always-on cost — the lab stayed for private services.
6. Failures I remember Single disk, no backup — one bad apt upgrade and a weekend restore from scratch. Exposing admin ports — learned to put admin UIs behind VPN only. Thermal noise — the R710 taught me to care about fan curves before “server” means “bedroom adjacent.” 7. Where it landed A homelab is a sandbox for platform instincts: automate installs, document topology, assume failure. Related today: MediaBoxDockerCompose[1] and install scripts on the main CV project list.
8. Related posts MediaBox homelab — Docker stack notes — compose, ports, and Proxmox helper-scripts Renpho scale + Home Assistant — another “own your data at home” project Skate rack — CAD to plywood — physical builds between cable runs Caddy on AWS — same reverse-proxy ideas, different bill
summary: Homelab evolution — Dell R710, closet wiring, Docker stacks, Caddy, WireGuard, Proxmox, and why I still draw the network on the wall.

BullETS LibraryCI Pythonaiohttppython-dotenvunittestGitHub ActionsPyPI BullETS is a Python package for developing algorithmic trading strategies: you subclass a strategy, attach a data source and let a runner replay the market. It is an AlgoÉTS project, published on PyPI under that name, for Python developers who want to test a trading idea on historical prices without first writing the market replay, order handling and data access themselves.
Overview A strategy extends Strategy (src/bullets/strategy.py) and overrides three hooks: on_start, on_resolution and on_finish. Runner (src/bullets/runner.py) builds the list of moments between the start and end dates at daily, hourly or minute resolution, skipping weekends, US market holidays (src/bullets/utils/holiday_date_util.py) and hours outside 9:30 to 16:00. At each moment it updates the shared timestamp, calls the strategy, then lets the portfolio check pending orders.
Portfolio (src/bullets/portfolio/portfolio.py) holds cash, holdings and the transaction log. A market order is filled at a simulated price: at daily resolution the price moves toward the day’s high by the slippage percentage (25 % by default), and a flat transaction fee (1 by default) is added. Each Transaction records its status (successful, insufficient funds or symbol not found) and logs itself.
Prices and fundamentals come from FmpDataSource (src/bullets/data_source/data_source_fmp.py), which calls the Financial Modeling Prep API with aiohttp, caches price points per symbol and also reads income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements and symbol lists. Indicators (src/bullets/data_indicators/indicators.py) computes moving averages and oscillators from the same source.
Getting started Register at Financial Modeling Prep for an API key, then install the package in a virtual environment:
python3 -m venv bot-env source bot-env/bin/activate pip install BullETS The README’s minimal strategy buys five AAPL shares at each resolution:
from bullets.strategy import Strategy, Resolution from bullets.runner import Runner from bullets.data_source.data_source_fmp import FmpDataSource from datetime import datetime class MyStrategy(Strategy): def on_resolution(self): self.portfolio.market_order("AAPL", 5) resolution = Resolution.DAILY data_source = FmpDataSource("Insert your key here", resolution) strategy = MyStrategy(resolution=resolution, start_time=datetime(2019, 3, 5), end_time=datetime(2019, 4, 22), starting_balance=5000, data_source=data_source) Runner(strategy).start() To work on the library itself, clone it, install it in editable mode and copy .env.sample to .env with your FMP_TOKEN:
git clone https://github.com/AlgoETS/BullETS cd BullETS pip install -e . python -m unittest discover src/test Repository guide src/bullets/strategy.py defines the Strategy base class and input validation. src/bullets/runner.py replays market moments and prints the end-of-backtest summary. src/bullets/portfolio/ holds Portfolio, Holding and Transaction. src/bullets/data_source/ contains the data source interface, the FMP implementation and the records for prices and financial statements. src/bullets/data_indicators/indicators.py implements the technical indicators. src/bullets/utils/ computes US market holidays and market-day offsets. src/bullets/logger.py provides coloured console logging with adjustable levels. src/test/ contains unittest suites for market hours, holidays, the portfolio and a full strategy run. .github/workflows/ runs lint and tests on pull requests and merges, and publishes to PyPI on release. Features strategy hooks for start, each resolution and finish; daily, hourly and minute resolutions with US market hours and holidays; market, stop and limit orders with slippage and transaction fees; end-of-run log with final balance, cash, fees, profit percentage and remaining FMP calls; price history, income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements and symbol lists from FMP, cached per symbol; SMA, WMA, EMA, MACD, RSI, standard deviation and Bollinger Bands; flake8, unittest and Codecov in CI; PyPI release workflow. Limits The README lists data retrieval, portfolio management and backtesting as “upcoming features”, and the version in setup.py is 0.1.1; the latest commit in the repository dates from March 2022. Slippage only applies at daily resolution; the strategy logs a warning otherwise. buy_limit_order and sell_limit_order add their orders to the stop-order lists, and filled stop or limit orders are not removed from their lists, so they can trigger again at later resolutions. The runner loop stops only when it lands exactly on end_time, so the end date must be reachable in whole resolution steps. Most tests call the live FMP API with FMP_TOKEN, so they need a key and network access. Only Financial Modeling Prep is implemented as a data source. Sources GitHub repository README src/bullets/runner.py src/bullets/strategy.py src/bullets/portfolio/portfolio.py src/bullets/data_source/data_source_fmp.py src/bullets/data_indicators/indicators.py
summary: BullETS is an AlgoÉTS Python library for writing stock trading strategies and backtesting them on Financial Modeling Prep data.
title: BullETS: a Python library for backtesting trading strategies

Kelly_RM NotebooksKelly criterion PythonJupyterbacktesting.pypandasNumPyhttpxAltairseaborn Kelly_RM is an AlgoÉTS research repository about risk management with the Kelly criterion, the rule that sets a bet size from the probability of winning and the payoff ratio. Its root README is empty; the code pairs a coin-flip simulation of Kelly betting with a notebook that backtests an RSI strategy, measures win odds per ticker and turns them into a Kelly fraction. It suits readers who want to see how the formula behaves before applying it to a strategy.
Overview Kelly_game/betting_strategies.py defines BaseGame, a repeated biased coin-flip game. Subclasses only decide the wager: Kelly bets the optimal fraction of wealth, KellyWithAnEstimate waits ten flips and bets on the observed frequency, ConstantDollar bets a fixed amount and BetLikeADummy bets big after three tails. The class plots wealth paths, simulates growth-rate distributions and draws expected growth against the fixed fraction wagered, with the Kelly point marked. Kelly_game/Playing the Game.ipynb runs the four strategies side by side; it describes itself as companion code for a video on the Kelly criterion.
sandbox/Main strategy.ipynb applies the idea to trading. It downloads price histories through src/data.py (Financial Modeling Prep and Binance helpers built on src/request_api.py), splits each series into three years of training data and an unseen remainder, and optimizes RsiOscillator from src/strategy.py with backtesting.py. From the resulting trade tables it computes, per ticker, the win probability and the mean and variance of win and loss sizes, keeps tickers seen in both periods, then applies f* = (p·b − q)/b with b = mean win / mean loss.
Getting started The French project description in docs/README.md gives the install step:
pip install -r requirements.txt jupyter notebook Set FMP_API_KEY (and BINANCE_API_KEY for the Binance helper) in the environment; src/config.py reads them. The notebooks also import packages that are not in requirements.txt, such as pandas_ta, scipy, sympy and altair; environment.yml is a full conda export that adds pandas-ta and SciPy but not every import.
Repository guide Kelly_game/betting_strategies.py contains the coin-flip game and its betting strategies. Kelly_game/Playing the Game.ipynb compares the strategies with Altair charts. sandbox/Main strategy.ipynb runs the RSI optimization, odds estimation and Kelly fraction. src/data.py, src/request_api.py and src/config.py fetch prices from FMP and Binance. src/strategy.py defines the Ema and RsiOscillator backtesting.py strategies. src/signal.py draws support and resistance lines with trendln and an R² threshold. docs/README.md is the French project description; docs/Kelle_complement.pdf is a reference paper on optimal trading under parameter uncertainty with a Monte Carlo approach. docs/notebook/strategy.ipynb is an empty placeholder. Features Kelly, estimated-Kelly, constant-dollar and “bet big after tails” strategies on a simulated coin; wealth-path charts, growth-rate histograms and expected growth versus wager fraction; FMP stock and crypto history and Binance futures klines through httpx; RSI parameter grid search with a seaborn heatmap; per-ticker win probability and win/loss size statistics on training and unseen data; Kelly fraction per retained ticker. Limits The root README.md is empty. docs/README.md describes risk limits in config.py, volatility adjustment, a user interface and a main script; none of these are in the code, and src/config.py only holds API keys and base URLs. Dependencies are incomplete: pandas_ta, trendln, fmp_python, scikit-learn, scipy, sympy and altair are imported but not listed in requirements.txt. sandbox/Main strategy.ipynb inserts a hard-coded Windows path into sys.path and calls the crypto price helper for S&P 500 stock symbols. It uses DataFrame.append, which pandas 2 removed, and its consistency filters are set to −1, which disables them. In src/strategy.py, the Ema strategy computes its 150-period line with the 80-period parameter. There are no tests, although pytest is in requirements-dev.txt. Results depend on saved notebook state and live API data; the repository does not record them. Sources GitHub repository Project description (docs/README.md) Kelly_game/betting_strategies.py sandbox/Main strategy.ipynb src/data.py src/strategy.py
summary: Kelly_RM holds AlgoÉTS notebooks that simulate Kelly betting and estimate trade odds from RSI backtests to compute a Kelly fraction.
title: Kelly_RM: Kelly criterion experiments for trade sizing

LegosTracker Notebooks and data PythonJupyterPlaywrightPydanticpandasscikit-learnMatplotlibBeautifulSoup LegosTracker is an AlgoÉTS data project that looks at LEGO sets as a market: the Rebrickable catalog says which sets, parts and themes exist, and a BrickEconomy scraper adds the prices sets fetch over time. It is meant for collectors and data science readers who want to explore the catalog or test simple price models on one set. The article Economics of LEGO Sets with Data Science tells the story with charts.
Overview brickeconomy.py reads set numbers from set_list.txt and drives a visible Chromium window with Playwright. For each set it searches BrickEconomy, opens the matching page and extracts the chart rows embedded in the page script: the value history goes to <set>_history.csv and, when present, the four-band price series to <set>_new.csv. It then reads the details, pricing, quick buy, predictions, facts and subtheme panels into Pydantic models and appends them to lego_sets.csv. brickeconomy.ipynb holds the same code with the install commands.
general.ipynb loads the Rebrickable tables in datasets/ (colors, inventories, parts, sets, themes and their links) and plots grouped counts. analyse.ipynb cleans the scraped data/lego_sets.csv and the data/001-1_*.csv files for the 1965 set 001-1, fits linear and gradient boosting regressions on the price history, projects them to 2030, runs a Monte Carlo simulation on log returns and charts yearly gains and the four price bands. price.ipynb takes a personal mycollection.csv, looks up retail and current values on BrickEconomy with requests and BeautifulSoup, and writes updated_mycollection.csv.
Getting started brickeconomy.ipynb installs the scraper dependencies:
pip install playwright asyncio pydantic aiohttp playwright install python brickeconomy.py The script writes its CSV files in the current directory; analyse.ipynb reads them from data/. The notebooks need pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, seaborn and scikit-learn (installed by the first cell of analyse.ipynb), plus requests and BeautifulSoup for price.ipynb:
pip install pandas matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn numpy jupyter notebook Repository guide brickeconomy.py is the Playwright scraper for BrickEconomy set pages. set_list.txt lists the set numbers to scrape (001-1 to 0016-1 and 002-1). data/ holds scraped output: lego_sets.csv and one _history.csv per set, plus 001-1_new.csv. datasets/ holds the Rebrickable exports as CSV and .csv.gz; the README documents their columns, and images/downloads_schema_v3.webp shows the schema. general.ipynb explores the Rebrickable catalog. analyse.ipynb cleans scraped prices and models the history of set 001-1. price.ipynb updates the values of the sets in mycollection.csv. Features scrape BrickEconomy value history, price bands and set panels for a list of sets; explore Rebrickable colors, inventories, parts, sets and themes; compare scraped prices across sets (lowest, highest, average); fit linear and gradient boosting regressions on a set’s price history and project them; simulate future prices with a Monte Carlo model on log returns; update the current value of a personal collection. Limits There is no requirements file; dependencies come from !pip install cells in the notebooks. The scraper depends on BrickEconomy’s page structure and CSS selectors, runs a visible browser and stops with an error when a search returns no link. Output files are written in the working directory, not in data/, so they must be moved before running analyse.ipynb. The scraped data covers nine sets; the price models work on a single set (001-1) and are illustrations, not forecasts. price.ipynb reads only the first table of the BrickEconomy search page and defines a TAX_RATE constant that it never uses. The Rebrickable exports are a dated snapshot; the repository has no script to refresh them. Sources GitHub repository README brickeconomy.py analyse.ipynb general.ipynb price.ipynb Exploring the data of LEGO history, linked from the README
summary: LegosTracker combines Rebrickable catalog exports, a Playwright scraper for BrickEconomy prices and notebooks that model LEGO set values.
title: LegosTracker: LEGO catalog data and set price history

MarkokChainMonteCarlo NotebooksMonte Carlo PythonJupyterbacktesting.pypandasNumPySciPyhttpxscikit-learn MarkokChainMonteCarlo is an AlgoÉTS research repository that backtests investment strategies with stochastic price simulations. Its notebooks estimate Apple (AAPL) price paths with a forward Monte Carlo model and a Markov chain over price ranges, then use those simulations inside a backtesting.py strategy compared with buy and hold. The forward Monte Carlo part is explained step by step in Predicting Stock Prices with Monte Carlo Simulations.
Overview mcmc.ipynb and backtest.ipynb share the same opening: an httpx helper downloads the full AAPL daily history from Financial Modeling Prep, and the data is split at 2023-01-01 into a training part and a hold-out part. monte_carlo_simulation estimates drift and volatility from log returns and propagates prices with random shocks; mcmc.ipynb adds variants with rolling volatility, occasional extreme moves and an optional stochastic drift, and plots 364-day projections with 1,000 or 10,000 paths. A Markov chain is built by cutting training closes into $10 bins from 0 to 200, counting bin-to-bin moves with pandas.crosstab and sampling a sequence with markov_chain_simulation. The notebook ends with a linear regression on the day index.
backtest.ipynb defines MCMCStrategy: it simulates paths and Markov states when the backtest starts, buys when the last simulated state is 0, and exits on a 5 % stop loss or when the close reaches a take-profit price drawn from a simulated path. BuyAndHoldStrategy serves as the baseline. Both run with 10,000 in cash, a 0.2 % commission and exclusive orders on the two periods. proto.ipynb is the first prototype on randomly generated prices, and output/MCMCStrategy.html is a saved backtesting.py chart.
Getting started The README installs the libraries with:
pip install panda lxml bs4 httpx backtesting yfinance pandas_ta scipy rich TA-Lib requirements.txt pins a smaller set (backtesting, httpx, numpy, pandas, pandas-ta). The notebooks also use Matplotlib and scikit-learn. Put your own Financial Modeling Prep key in the FMP_API_KEY cell, then open the notebooks:
jupyter notebook backtest.ipynb Repository guide mcmc.ipynb covers data split, Monte Carlo variants, the Markov chain, plots and the linear regression. backtest.ipynb repeats the simulations and runs MCMCStrategy and BuyAndHoldStrategy. proto.ipynb is the prototype on synthetic prices. output/MCMCStrategy.html is a saved backtest chart. images/ holds the README illustrations. Algo Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)_.pdf is a PDF document stored with the code. Features AAPL daily history from Financial Modeling Prep, split at 2023-01-01; forward Monte Carlo price paths, with rolling-volatility and extreme-move variants; Markov chain over $10 price bins with an empirical transition matrix; backtesting.py strategy using simulated states and take-profit levels; buy and hold baseline on the same periods; linear trend fit on the day index. Limits Despite the name, there is no Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler (such as Metropolis–Hastings) in the code; the notebooks combine a forward Monte Carlo simulation with a separate Markov chain. MCMCStrategy simulates once, at the start of the backtest, over the full series and reads the last element of a fixed state list, so its entry condition does not change from bar to bar. It also starts the chain from a hard-coded state 0. The transition matrix only covers closes from 0 to 200, with one open bin above. An FMP API key is written in the notebooks; replace it with your own. The README install line contains panda instead of pandas, and requirements.txt does not list every import. The notebooks do not keep their backtest outputs, and the results depend on random draws without a fixed seed (except in proto.ipynb). Sources GitHub repository README mcmc.ipynb backtest.ipynb proto.ipynb
summary: AlgoÉTS notebooks that simulate AAPL prices with Monte Carlo paths and a Markov chain, then backtest a strategy built on them against buy and hold.
title: MarkokChainMonteCarlo: Monte Carlo and Markov chain backtests

PolyFEMBlenderPlugin Blender add-onDocker PythonBlender 4.2PolyFEMTetWildmeshioGitHub Actions PolyFEMBlenderPlugin is an experimental Blender extension that turns selected objects, materials and contact settings into a PolyFEM JSON setup and runs the finite-element simulation without leaving Blender. It was written for the ÉTS lab’s simulation work and is published under ETSim, for people who prepare scenes in Blender but solve them with PolyFEM.
Overview polyfem/__init__.py registers one panel, the property groups and the operators. On registration it also installs meshio with pip into Blender’s user modules folder.
polyfem/panels/polyfem_json.py draws the PolyFEM panel in the Physics tab of the Properties editor: execution mode (Docker or executable) for PolyFEM and TetWild, the selected objects with their materials and export format, then collapsible sections for export, contact, time, space, boundary conditions, materials, solver and output settings. polyfem/operators/create_polyfem_json.py exports each mesh (STL, OBJ, or MSH through TetWild) and writes the PolyFEM JSON file with geometry, materials, contact, time, boundary_conditions, solver and output blocks. polyfem/operators/run_polyfem.py starts PolyFEM in a background thread, either docker run antoinebou12/polyfem --json /data/<file> with the project folder mounted on /data, or a local executable. Its Render Animation operator reads the step_*.vtu results, adds the solution displacement, converts each step to OBJ with meshio and keyframes the visibility of each imported mesh. polyfem/properties/polyfem.py holds the settings, including material presets (steel, copper, aluminium and others), integrators (implicit Euler, explicit Euler, implicit Newmark) and Eigen linear solvers. Getting started The README installs the add-on from a zip of the polyfem/ folder: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install, then enable PolyFem. Blender 4.2 or later is required by blender_manifest.toml. The default execution mode uses Docker:
docker pull yixinhu/tetwild:latest docker pull antoinebou12/polyfem:latest The CI workflow builds the extension package with Blender’s own command:
blender --command extension build --source-dir polyfem --output-dir docs blender --command extension server-generate --repo-dir=docs --html Repository guide polyfem/ is the extension itself (blender_manifest.toml, __init__.py, operators/, panels/, properties/). polyfem/operators/create_polyfem_json.py handles mesh export, TetWild, materials, Docker image pulls and the JSON file. polyfem/operators/run_polyfem.py runs PolyFEM, imports results, opens the PolyFEM documentation and clears the cache. polyfem/properties/polyfem.py defines every panel field and preset. .github/workflows/build.yml builds the extension zip and an extension repository index (docs/index.json), then deploys docs/ to the gh-pages branch. docs/ holds built packages polyfem-1.0.10.zip and polyfem-1.0.11.zip with their index. zip-plugin.py and download-wheels.py are helper scripts to zip the add-on and download wheels for meshio, trimesh and tetgen. Features Assign elastic material properties (E, ν, ρ) to objects from presets or custom values. Export meshes to STL or OBJ, or tetrahedralize them to MSH with TetWild in Docker or as a local executable. Set contact (dhat, friction coefficient, epsv), time integration, boundary-condition method and right-hand side, linear solver and ParaView output options. Write a complete PolyFEM JSON file, with optional export of selected objects only. Run PolyFEM through Docker or a local executable without blocking the Blender interface. Import VTU time steps back as a keyframed mesh sequence. Limits The README calls the add-on experimental and lists crashes with complex geometry and mesh-export edge cases as known issues. The panel is registered in the Properties editor’s Physics tab, while the README describes a 3D Viewport sidebar tab. FBX and glTF appear in the export menu but the operator rejects them. blender_manifest.toml lists only windows-x64 as a platform, and the add-on needs Docker or local PolyFEM and TetWild builds. The README states GPL-3.0, while LICENSE and the manifest state MIT. The README badges and file tree refer to an older repository name and to a panels/poly_fem.py file that is not in the tree. There are no tests. The workflow only builds and publishes the package. Sources GitHub repository README polyfem/blender_manifest.toml polyfem/operators/create_polyfem_json.py polyfem/operators/run_polyfem.py .github/workflows/build.yml
summary: Blender 4.2 add-on that exports meshes and physics settings to a PolyFEM JSON file, runs PolyFEM through Docker and imports the results.
title: PolyFEMBlenderPlugin: PolyFEM simulations from a Blender scene

Salary Data analysisAPIDocker PythonpandasPolarsPyPDF2JupyterFastAPIBeautifulSouppre-commit Salary is an AlgoÉTS data project about pay in Canada. It turns recruitment-firm salary guides (PDF) and federal wage tables (CSV) into data frames, then compares jobs across provinces, regions and experience levels. It is useful to anyone who wants to see how a job such as cloud architect is paid from one region to another, and to readers interested in extracting tables from PDF reports.
Overview The PDF path is handled by one script per guide edition. src/pdf_salary_scraper_2023_1.py and src/pdf_salary_scraper_2024_1.py read a guide in data/pdf/ with PyPDF2, track the current province and region from fixed name lists, split each line into a job title and three salary ranges (entry, mid and senior) and save the result as a pickle in data/pickle/. src/pdf.py is an earlier PyMuPDF experiment that tags text by font size to find headings.
src/wages_in_time.py loads the Job Bank wage files data/csv/wage_2012.csv to wage_2022.csv with Polars, harmonizes column names across years, caches the combined table in data/pickle/wages.pkl and prints the best-paid jobs per year and the best-paid engineering jobs per province. src/stackoverflow_scraper.py scrapes the salary table of the 2022 Stack Overflow survey.
Analysis happens in sandbox/salary_exploration_2023.ipynb and sandbox/salary_exploration_2024.ipynb, with helper versions of the same functions in src/analyse.py: split the ranges, compute means per level, rank jobs, filter engineering and Québec jobs, compare one job across regions and provinces, and find the jobs with the widest regional spread. api/app.py exposes the 2023 and 2024 pickles as JSON through FastAPI, and web/ holds two static HTML pages.
Getting started The README lists these steps:
pip install -r requirements.txt python src/pdf.py jupyter notebook Run the extraction scripts from the repository root, since they use paths such as data/pdf/2023_salary_guide.pdf:
python src/pdf_salary_scraper_2023_1.py python src/wages_in_time.py api/setup.md describes Docker and Vercel deployment of the API; locally, it can be started with uvicorn from the api/ directory:
cd api uvicorn app:app --reload Repository guide src/pdf_salary_scraper_2023_1.py and src/pdf_salary_scraper_2024_1.py extract the 2023 and 2024 guides (the README names Randstad as the source); the _2 and generic_wip scripts are function-based variants. src/wages_in_time.py combines the 2012–2022 Job Bank wage tables. src/stackoverflow_scraper.py scrapes the Stack Overflow survey salary table. src/analyse.py and src/utils.py hold analysis and pickle helpers; src/__init__.py lists provinces and regions. sandbox/ contains the 2023 and 2024 exploration notebooks and a 2023-to-2024 comparison. data/pdf/, data/csv/, data/pickle/ and data/geo/ hold source guides from several recruitment firms, wage tables, extracted pickles and province shapefiles; data/csv/README.md documents the wage columns. api/ contains the FastAPI app, Dockerfile, Compose file and deployment notes. web/index.html shows 2023 results as static text; web/job_search.html is a search form mock-up. Features extract job, province, region and entry, mid and senior ranges from salary guide PDFs; combine eleven years of Job Bank wage tables into one Polars data frame; rank jobs by maximum salary, overall, per year, per province and for engineering roles; compare one job across regions and provinces and find the widest regional gaps; scrape Stack Overflow survey salaries; serve the extracted 2023 and 2024 guides as JSON through FastAPI. Limits The README states the goal of a salary prediction model by region, experience and education; the repository contains extraction and exploration code, but no model. The README commands name src/pdf_salary_scraper.py and a root stackoverflow_scraper.py, which do not exist under those names. requirements.txt misses PyMuPDF, Polars and BeautifulSoup, which the scripts import; src/wages_in_time.py uses an older Polars API. Province and region come from the first name in a fixed list found anywhere on the page, the entry range joins the low of the first pair with the high of the second, and four-range lines are skipped. The README and web/index.html list a bilingual receptionist at $713,000 as the top 2023 salary, which points to extraction errors. src/wages_in_time.py annualizes hourly wages with 40 × 45 hours in one function and 45 × 45 in another, and flags the 2017 and 2018 files as badly formatted. Deployment files disagree: vercel.json builds a root app.py while the app is api/app.py, the Dockerfile runs unicorn on port 8000 while Compose maps 5000, and the API reads pickles through ../data relative paths. src/test.py imports functions that do not exist, and setup.py still points to a code package directory and a template description. Sources GitHub repository README src/pdf_salary_scraper_2024_1.py src/wages_in_time.py sandbox/salary_exploration_2023.ipynb api/app.py data/csv/README.md
summary: Salary extracts Canadian salary guide PDFs and Job Bank wage tables with Python, then compares pay by job, province and region in notebooks.
title: Salary: exploring Canadian salary guides and wage data

SimilityVectorEmbedding NotebooksDocker PythonJupyterPostgreSQLpgvectorQdrantNeo4jSentence TransformersLangChainOllamaGradio SimilityVectorEmbedding is a set of Jupyter notebooks that turn a movie catalog into embeddings and look for similar films with several storage and ranking approaches. It is an AlgoÉTS repository for readers who want to see vector search applied to real movie records. The article Exploring movie similarities with vector search algorithms tells the same work as a story, with the original demo animations.
Overview Each folder pairs a notebook with the database it needs. All of them read a movies.json file whose records use French keys (titre, annee, genre, realisateur, role, synopsis …) under films.film.
postgres/0.simple.ipynb is the shortest full path: it builds one text per film (title, year, genres, actors, director, summary, country, language, writers), encodes it with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 using mean pooling, normalizes the vectors and inserts them into a movies table with a VECTOR(384) column. Titles typed by the user are matched with pg_trgm before cosine similarity ranks the rest of the catalog. It also averages several titles, weights titles by rating, plots the scores and ends with a Gradio interface. postgres/1.create_table.ipynb encodes the same catalog with five configurations (BART, GTE, MiniLM-L12, RoBERTa and e5-large) and stores one vector column per model. postgres/3.LLMS.ipynb embeds a natural-language question, runs a pgvector <=> cosine query and sends the table schema to a LangChain chain backed by Ollama (llama2:13b-chat). qdrant/0.simple.ipynb upserts 384-dimension vectors in batches of 100 into a cosine collection, searches it, and projects the vectors with t-SNE and k-means. bm25/0.bm25.ipynb ranks films by keywords with rank_bm25, without embeddings. neo4j/1.create_db.ipynb loads movies and people as a graph and scores neighbours by shared genres, directors, writers and actors. Getting started The notebooks install their own packages with !pip install cells. Start the database for the notebook you want to run, then open Jupyter:
git clone https://github.com/AlgoETS/SimilityVectorEmbedding.git cd SimilityVectorEmbedding/postgres docker-compose up -d jupyter notebook postgres/docker-compose.yml builds PostgreSQL with pgvector compiled from source and pg_trgm, on port 5432. The qdrant/ and neo4j/ folders each have their own docker-compose.yml (Qdrant on 6333/6334, Neo4j on 7474/7687 with APOC and Graph Data Science). neo4j/install_ollama.sh installs Ollama on Linux for the LLM notebook.
Repository guide postgres/0.simple.ipynb: MiniLM embeddings, title matching, single/multiple/rated searches, bar chart and Gradio UI. postgres/1.create_table.ipynb: five embedding models stored side by side in PostgreSQL. postgres/3.LLMS.ipynb: question embedding, pgvector query and LangChain + Ollama prompt. postgres/Dockerfile, postgres/docker-compose.yml, postgres/init-db.sh: database image and extension setup. qdrant/0.simple.ipynb, qdrant/docker-compose.yml: the Qdrant version of the search, with clustering plots. bm25/0.bm25.ipynb: keyword ranking baseline. neo4j/1.create_db.ipynb, neo4j/docker-compose.yml, neo4j/personnes.json: graph model of films and people. */movies.json: the movie catalog, copied into each folder. Features build an embedding text from several movie fields, with English stopwords removed from title and summary; compare five Hugging Face / Sentence Transformers models on the same catalog; store vectors in PostgreSQL with pgvector and match approximate titles with pg_trgm; search by one title, the mean of several titles, or a rating-weighted mix of titles; run the same idea on Qdrant, then on BM25 keywords and a Neo4j graph for comparison; ask questions through a local LLM grounded on the movies table; view results as bar charts, t-SNE/k-means plots, graph views and a Gradio page. Limits The README asks for pip install -r requirements.txt and a Similarity_Vector_Embedding.ipynb notebook; neither file is in the repository. Dependencies come from the !pip install cells. The README schema shows a single VECTOR(768) column; the notebooks create per-model columns (384 or 1024 dimensions). postgres/init-db.sh creates an extension named pgvector, while the notebooks create vector, the name pgvector registers. Notebooks drop and recreate the movies table and the Qdrant collection, and use hard-coded local credentials (postgres/postgres, neo4j/password). The LLM notebook needs a running Ollama server with llama2:13b-chat; the Gradio cell uses launch(share=True), which opens a public share link. There are no tests. Saved notebook outputs show past runs, not benchmarks. Sources GitHub repository README postgres/0.simple.ipynb postgres/1.create_table.ipynb postgres/3.LLMS.ipynb qdrant/0.simple.ipynb neo4j/1.create_db.ipynb
summary: Jupyter notebooks that embed a movie catalog and compare pgvector, Qdrant, BM25, Neo4j and a local LLM for finding similar films.
title: SimilityVectorEmbedding: movie similarity with vector search

Simulateur Web appAPIDocker PythonDjangoDjango REST frameworkChannelsDaphneCeleryPostgreSQLRedisMinIOOllamaWagtail Simulateur is a stock-market simulation platform built with Django: an admin prepares a scenario with fictional companies, news and events, and teams of players trade the simulated stocks while prices move in real time. It is an AlgoÉTS repository for groups that want to run a market game together, with an admin interface that controls the settings and the flow of each simulation.
Overview The Django project lives in simulateur/. simulateur/settings.py registers two local apps, simulation and backtesting, and uses SQLite unless DATABASE_ENGINE=postgresql is set.
Price engine. simulation/logic/simulation_manager.py holds one SimulationManager per simulation. While the state is ongoing, it sleeps for the configured timer step, skips New York market-closed hours if asked, and writes an OHLC candle per stock from the chosen noise model (brownian, perlin, random_walk, fbm, random or monte_carlo in logic/noise_patterns/). Each candle is stored as StockPriceHistory and pushed to the WebSocket layer. Lifecycle. manage.py start_simulation <ids> sets the simulations to ongoing, polls their state every five seconds and applies changed settings. The states are initialized, created, published, ongoing, stopped and finished. Live updates. simulation/channels/consumers.py serves ws/simulation/<room>/ and relays stock updates, news, events and triggers to the game dashboard. Trading. simulation/api/portfolio.py handles buy and sell orders against the latest price and the portfolio balance, and exposes holdings, performance and leaderboards. Scenario authoring. The admin dashboard walks through five steps (settings, companies and stocks, teams, events, review). simulation/api/ai_llm.py can draft news, events, triggers, companies or whole scenarios with an Ollama model (OLLAMA_MODEL, llama3 by default). Backtesting app. backtesting/ adds chart search, strategy management and a sandbox page, data endpoints named for FMP, CoinGecko and yfinance, and Celery tasks for strategy runs. run.py ties it together: it installs requirements, applies migrations, creates a superadmin, seeds the CSV files in data/, then starts Daphne (and optionally simulations and the Wagtail CMS on port 8001) in separate threads. In the Docker image, run.sh runs the same migrate, seed and superadmin steps before run.py --start-simulation 1.
Getting started The README’s Docker Compose path runs Django, Celery, PostgreSQL, a Redis-compatible Dragonfly server and MinIO. The compose file and its .env live in simulateur/:
cd simulateur cp env-default .env docker compose --profile all down docker compose --profile all up -d --build Without Docker, use run.py (the README writes python3 -m run.py, but the script is run directly):
cd simulateur python3 run.py --install python3 run.py --start-simulation 1 --install creates a local-development superadmin with the README’s sample admin/admin login and seeds the database; change it before exposing the app. Another superadmin can be created with your own values:
python3 manage.py createsuperadmin --username=<name> --password=<password> --email=<email> The Django test suite under simulation/tests/ runs with python3 manage.py test. Swagger and ReDoc pages are served at /swagger/ and /redoc/.
Repository guide simulateur/run.py: install, migrate, seed and start Daphne, simulations or the CMS. simulateur/simulateur/: settings, URL root, ASGI entry (asgi.py) and Celery app. simulateur/simulation/logic/: simulation loop, noise models, broker and buy/sell queue. simulateur/simulation/api/: REST views for companies, stocks, scenarios, simulation managers, news, events, triggers, teams, portfolios and AI generation. simulateur/simulation/channels/: WebSocket consumer and routing. simulateur/simulation/models/: scenario, company, stock, team, portfolio, order and settings models. simulateur/simulation/management/commands/: start_simulation, seed_database and createsuperadmin. simulateur/simulation/templates/: admin, game, team and user dashboards built from partials. simulateur/simulation/tests/: tests for the API, models, logic, channels and commands. simulateur/backtesting/: backtesting views, data APIs, models and Celery tasks. simulateur/cms/: a separate Wagtail project. simulateur/data/: CSV seed data (companies, stocks, scenarios, teams, users, events, triggers …). notebooks/: prototypes for the broker, agents, noise, charts and strategies. docs/diagrams/: PlantUML use-case and sequence diagrams. Features create companies with backstories, stocks, teams and user profiles; configure the timer step, fluctuation rate, market-hours closing and noise model per simulation; start, stop and finish simulations from the admin dashboard or the command line; stream OHLC candles, news, events and triggers to players over WebSockets; buy and sell stocks within a portfolio balance and follow holdings and performance; rank players and teams on leaderboards and invite players with team join links; draft scenario content with a local Ollama model; sign in with accounts or Google, GitHub, Microsoft and Notion through django-allauth; expose health checks, Prometheus metrics and an OpenAPI description. Limits The README lists Django 4.2.13; requirements.txt pins Django 5.0.8. The README badge says Python 3.12 while the Docker image uses Python 3.10. Price broadcasts are sent to WebSocket room 1 regardless of the simulation id, so only simulation 1 receives live updates as written. The dynamic trading mode relies on logic/broker.py, which imports the BuySellQueue module instead of the class and omits the simulation_manager argument; that path looks unfinished. The default mode is static. logic/noise_patterns/ also contains GBM, Heston, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and Vasicek models that the simulation manager does not offer. backtesting/batchbacktesting.py imports src.data and strategies modules that are not in the repository. The AI endpoints need a reachable Ollama server; entrypoint.sh starts one and pulls a model, but the Dockerfile and compose file do not use it. Defaults use weak demo credentials (admin/admin, minioadmin, postgres), and scripts/ contains a localhost certificate and key. Sources GitHub repository README simulateur/run.py simulateur/simulation/logic/simulation_manager.py simulateur/simulation/urls.py simulateur/simulation/api/portfolio.py simulateur/docker-compose.yml
summary: Simulateur is a Django platform where admins script market scenarios and teams trade simulated stocks with live WebSocket prices.
title: Simulateur: a Django stock-market simulation game

Sport-Arbitrage Static page HTMLJavaScriptTailwind CSSPythonJupyter Sport-Arbitrage is a small web calculator for sports-betting arbitrage: you enter the odds two betting sites give for the same match, and it tells you whether betting on opposite outcomes at both sites locks in a profit, and how to split the stake. It is an AlgoÉTS repository with a browser page and a Python notebook that run the same formulas.
Overview index.html is a single form styled with Tailwind CSS 2.2.19 from a CDN. All the logic is in script.js:
hasArbitrageOpportunity(odds) adds the inverses of the odds and reports an opportunity when the sum is below 1. calculateArbitragePercentage returns (1 − Σ 1/odds) × 100. calculateOptimalStakes splits the total investment in proportion to each inverse odd, so every outcome returns the same amount. calculateTotalReturn and calculateGuaranteedProfit give the return per outcome and the smallest return minus the investment. calculateArbitrage() reads the form, tests two cross-site pairings (win at site 1 with loss at site 2, and loss at site 1 with win at site 2) and adds a draw to each pairing in three-outcome mode, then writes one result card per opportunity. arbitrage.ipynb contains the same functions in Python, with sample odds hard-coded in the first cell.
Getting started Nothing needs to be built. Clone the repository and open the page in a browser (the Tailwind stylesheet loads from jsDelivr, so the page needs network access to look right):
git clone https://github.com/AlgoETS/Sport-Arbitrage.git cd Sport-Arbitrage Then open index.html, choose 2 or 3 odds, fill in the odds and the total investment, and click Calculate. To run the Python version:
jupyter notebook arbitrage.ipynb Repository guide index.html: the calculator form, instructions and result area. script.js: field toggling, arbitrage test, stake split, returns and profit display. arbitrage.ipynb: Python version of the formulas for the two-outcome case. style.css: basic layout styles (not referenced by index.html). Features switch between two-outcome (win/loss) and three-outcome (win/loss/draw) markets; test cross-site pairings for an arbitrage with the inverse-odds sum; show the arbitrage percentage, optimal stakes, return per outcome and guaranteed profit; run entirely in the browser, with no server or account; check the same math in a Jupyter notebook. Limits Only two fixed pairings are tested. In three-outcome mode, the draw from site 1 always joins win at site 1 and loss at site 2, and the draw from site 2 joins loss at site 1 and win at site 2; other mixes are never tried. The formulas assume decimal odds, and the form does not validate input: empty fields produce NaN. Stakes are not rounded and ignore fees, betting limits and odds changes, so the “guaranteed profit” holds only if every bet is accepted at the entered odds. style.css is not linked from the page, and the notebook covers only the two-outcome case. There are no tests. Sources GitHub repository README index.html script.js arbitrage.ipynb
summary: Sport-Arbitrage is a one-page calculator that checks odds from two betting sites for an arbitrage and computes stakes and guaranteed profit.
title: Sport-Arbitrage: a sports-betting arbitrage calculator

TradingViewBuilder Scripts Pine ScriptTradingView TradingViewBuilder is a collection of TradingView indicators and strategies written in Pine Script, one file per technique. It is an AlgoÉTS repository for traders who want readable starting points for common technical rules that they can paste into the Pine Editor, apply to a chart and adjust.
Overview Files ending in .indicator declare a study() (or indicator()) that only plots values. Files ending in .strategy declare a strategy() that also places strategy.entry orders on crossover rules:
Technique Strategy rule Files EMA crossover Long when EMA 9 crosses above EMA 21, short on the opposite cross ema.strategy, ema.indcator SMA crossover Buy when SMA 10 crosses above SMA 20, close on the opposite cross mac.strategy MACD Long/short on MACD (12, 26) crossing its 9-period signal line macd.strategy, macd.indicator RSI Long when RSI 14 crosses above 30, short when it crosses below 70 rsi.strategy, rsi.indicator Bollinger Bands Long when the close crosses above the lower band (20, 2σ), short below the upper band bollingerbands.strategy Linear regression Same band rule around a 20-bar linear regression ± 2 standard deviations linearregression.strategy, linearregression.indicator Relative Vigor Index Long/short when RVI (10) crosses its 4-period signal line rvi.strategy, rvi.indicator Standard deviation Bands at close ± 20-bar standard deviation standarddeviation.strategy, standarddeviation.indicator TimeSeriesMomentumEffect.strategy is a larger draft: it lists 60 futures contracts, measures each one’s return over 12 × 21 bars, goes long winners and short losers, and sizes positions with a volatility target and a leverage cap.
Getting started There is nothing to install. The README’s steps are:
Log in to TradingView and open the Pine Editor tab at the bottom of a chart. Copy the contents of a .indicator or .strategy file from this repository and paste it into the editor. Click Add to Chart (and Save to keep the script under a name). Use the gear icon next to the script label to change lengths, sources, levels and colours. Repository guide *.indicator (and ema.indcator): plotting-only versions of EMA, linear regression, MACD, RSI, RVI and standard deviation. *.strategy: trading versions with entry rules for EMA, SMA crossover (mac), MACD, RSI, Bollinger Bands, linear regression, RVI and standard deviation. TimeSeriesMomentumEffect.strategy: multi-asset time-series momentum draft. README.md: list of techniques and the TradingView setup steps. docs/about.md: placeholder page with a heading only. Features eight classic technical techniques, most available as both an indicator and a strategy; adjustable inputs (input()) for every length, multiplier and threshold; chart overlays: bands, moving averages, signal lines and overbought/oversold levels; a written-out time-series momentum idea with volatility targeting. Limits Most files target Pine Script v4. mac.strategy declares @version=5 but uses v4 calls, and ema.indcator declares @version=4 but uses v5 calls (indicator, input.int, ta.ema); either version header needs changing before they compile. standarddeviation.strategy compares close with close ± std; since the bands always sit on either side of the close, the crossover conditions never fire and the strategy places no trades as written. TimeSeriesMomentumEffect.strategy uses syntax that Pine does not accept (brace-delimited functions, length() on arrays), so it reads as pseudocode rather than a runnable script. The README calls RVI the “Relative Volatility Index”, but the code computes the Relative Vigor Index; mac.strategy is not listed in the README, and ema.indcator has a typo in its extension. Strategies enter and reverse on opposite signals (only mac.strategy closes instead); there are no stops, position sizing or commission settings, and the repository contains no backtest results. Sources GitHub repository README macd.strategy rsi.strategy bollingerbands.strategy TimeSeriesMomentumEffect.strategy
summary: TradingViewBuilder collects Pine Script indicators and strategies (EMA, MACD, RSI, Bollinger Bands, RVI …) to paste into TradingView.
title: TradingViewBuilder: Pine Script indicators and strategies

WearBlender Blender scenes BlenderShader nodesGeometry nodes WearBlender is a set of Blender scenes, published under ETSim, for learning and teaching how artists usually fake wear: worn edges, scratches, rotated normal maps, painted marks and proximity effects. It sits beside the ÉTS master’s research on wear in texture space, where wear comes from simulated contact rather than hand-built masks.
Overview The repository holds only .blend files, a README and an MIT licence. The README lists five themes. The node types stored in each file show how the scenes cover them:
Edge wear.blend: a worn-edge mask from Bevel and Geometry nodes, a color ramp and a roughness image texture on a plane. Scratched.blend: procedural micro-scratches on a Suzanne mesh from Voronoi and Noise textures, color ramps and Bump nodes. NormalRotation.blend: an image normal map whose vectors are turned with Vector Rotate and Vector Math nodes. WeightPainting.blend: geometry-node trees that read a painted attribute with Named Attribute, and a material that mixes shaders through an Attribute node. flowmap.blend: vector nodes that split and recombine coordinates to push a texture along a flow image. SurfaceCameraProjection.blend: a second camera, a CameraProjectionMaterial with an emission shader and a rigid-body world. Three more scenes, Sliding_cube.blend, Wrapping project.blend and flowmap_vector field.blend, are larger files. Their names suggest a sliding-cube setup, a wrapping test and a vector-field flowmap variant. The README does not describe them separately.
Getting started Nothing needs to be built. Clone the repository and open any file in Blender; the README says the scenes were tested in Blender 4.5 LTS.
git clone https://github.com/ETSim/WearBlender blender "WearBlender/Edge wear.blend" Then, as the README suggests, look at the Shader Editor or Geometry Nodes editor, toggle visibility or play the animation, and reuse the node setups in your own materials.
Repository guide Edge wear.blend covers curvature and bevel-based edge wear. Scratched.blend covers procedural scratches with bump. NormalRotation.blend covers rotating normal maps in a shader. WeightPainting.blend covers wear driven by painted attributes and geometry nodes. flowmap.blend and flowmap_vector field.blend cover texture flow maps. SurfaceCameraProjection.blend covers projecting a camera texture onto a surface. Sliding_cube.blend and Wrapping project.blend are additional scenes named after a sliding cube and a wrapping project. README.md lists the themes and how to use the files. Features Edge wear from curvature, bevel and color ramps. Procedural scratches from Voronoi and noise textures. Rotated normal maps for dynamic surface detail. Wear driven by painted attributes and geometry nodes. Flow-map texture offsets. Camera texture projection onto a surface. Limits The repository contains scenes only: no scripts, add-on or rendered previews. The README describes five themes but does not map them to file names, and it mentions a dynamic-paint scene without naming the file. The scenes reproduce artist-driven wear looks. They are not physical wear models. The files were saved by Blender 4.4 and 4.5, so older Blender versions may not open them. Sources GitHub repository README Edge wear.blend Scratched.blend WeightPainting.blend
summary: Example Blender files showing edge wear, scratches, rotated normal maps, flow maps and painted wear with shaders and geometry nodes.
title: WearBlender: Blender scenes for wear effects

WearMachine Hardware / CAD STEPSTLDXFInkscape SVG WearMachine collects the parts of the abrasion bench used in the ÉTS master’s research on wear in texture space: a sample slides on a rail under a chosen load, then is scanned with a GelSight sensor. The repository, published under ETSim, is for anyone who wants to rebuild or adapt the rig to evaluate wear, study friction or check simulations against measurements.
Overview The README states the goal and the components: a GelSight bench, custom fixtures (the CAD files in the repository), load sensors, linear actuators and a control and acquisition system. Only the fixtures are in the repository. They are organised in three part families, each available in up to four formats:
Rail: Rail, Rail_Holder, Rail_Ski, Pusher, Seperator, Holder Berring, plus a Base plate drawing, a nema17bracket_v2 motor bracket and a t8_nut lead-screw nut. The names point to a stepper motor and lead screw moving the sample along the rail. Weight: Weight Holder parts for 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1000 g that set the normal load on the sample. Gelsight_Holder: 30mm Sample Holder, 40mm Sample Holder and Benchtop Holder Square to hold samples under the GelSight sensor. Picture/Assembly.png is a 1:8 drawing sheet, dated March 2025, of the assembled frame: two rails and a crossbar with five sample holes of increasing size. Drawing/Mold/20240430_16_Holes.svg is an A4 Inkscape sheet with a 16-hole mold layout.
Getting started There is nothing to run. Pick the folder that matches what you want to do:
open the STEP files in Raw/ with a CAD tool (FreeCAD, Fusion, SolidWorks…) to change dimensions; slice the STL files in Print/ for 3D printing; use the DXF files in Drawing/ for flat outlines or laser cutting, and the PNG sheets in Picture/ as visual references. git clone https://github.com/ETSim/WearMachine ls WearMachine/Print/Rail WearMachine/Print/Weight WearMachine/Print/Gelsight_Holder Repository guide Raw/ holds STEP solids for the GelSight holders, the rail parts and most weight holders. Print/ holds STL meshes for printing, including the motor bracket and the T8 nut. Drawing/ holds DXF outlines for the two round GelSight holders, the rail parts (including Base.dxf) and all weight holders, plus the mold SVG. Picture/ holds PNG drawing sheets of individual parts and Assembly.png. README.md gives the purpose and the list of required components. Features Complete set of printable fixtures for a rail-guided sliding test. Seven weight holders from 10 g to 1000 g for repeatable normal loads. Two round sample holders (30 mm and 40 mm) and a square benchtop holder for GelSight capture. Editable STEP sources next to ready-to-print STL files. Measured surfaces from this kind of test are published in WearSurfacesDatasets, whose loads range from 10 to 200 g. Limits The README says the repository provides detailed build instructions, but it contains no assembly steps, bill of materials or hardware list beyond the component names. No firmware, wiring or control software is included for the actuators, load sensors or acquisition system the README lists. Formats are uneven: Base exists only as DXF, Holder Berring and Weight Holder 10g have no STEP file, and the motor bracket and nut have no STEP or drawing. The drawing sheets have empty title, material and tolerance fields. The repository has a Python .gitignore but no code. Sources GitHub repository README Picture/Assembly.png Raw/Rail/Rail.step Print/Rail/nema17bracket_v2.stl Drawing/Weight/Weight Holder 200g.dxf
summary: STEP, STL, DXF and drawing files for a small sliding-wear rig: rail, pusher, weight holders and GelSight sample holders.
title: WearMachine: CAD files for a GelSight wear bench

WearSurfacesDatasets DatasetAPI PythonParquetWebDatasetGit LFSOpenCVFastAPIWebGPU WearSurfacesDatasets publishes the surface textures captured during controlled wear tests, organised by material, abrasive grit, load and sliding distance. It is the public dataset of the ÉTS master’s research on wear in texture space, where it serves to compare simulated wear patterns with measured microgeometry, and it is published under ETSim for graphics and tribology researchers who need real wear progressions.
Overview Each measured state is one Parquet leaf:
data/parquet/<material>/<shape>/<direction>/S<grit>/<load>g/<distance>mm/data.parquet For example data/parquet/Cartboard/Raw/Normal/S60/200g/800mm/data.parquet. Each row stores one map as JPEG bytes in image_data, labelled by map_type; metadata.json lists ambient occlusion, bump, displacement, height, hillshade and normal maps. The same records are also packed as WebDataset archives data/shards/shard-0000.tar to shard-0839.tar.
data/parquet/sequences.json lists 20 wear timelines: cardboard at five loads (10 to 200 g, grit S60), foam, MDF (circle and line paths), PLA at several grits in linear and non-linear directions, soft wood, and unworn sandpaper references from S40 to S240.
On top of the data, the repository has three layers of tooling:
generate_datasets.py, read_datasets.py and generate_metadata.py (Typer CLIs) build Parquet and shards from a wear/ folder of PNG maps, extract them back, and write per-leaf and index metadata. alignment/ registers each sequence with a two-pass SIFT/ECC method (align.py), crops the common valid region, adds temporal Catmull-Rom midpoints (interpolate.py) and extrapolates future normal maps with an FFT plus SLERP model (extrapolate.py). bake.py runs it per sequence or for all of them and can repack the results. docs/index.html is a WebGPU material viewer that reads Parquet in the browser with parquet-wasm. docs/serve_local.py is a FastAPI server that serves the viewer and the data and exposes /api/datasets, /api/sequences and /api/align/sequence. Getting started From the README:
git clone https://github.com/ETSim/WearSurfacesDatasets cd WearSurfacesDatasets git lfs pull pip install -r requirements.txt python docs/serve_local.py # open http://127.0.0.1:8080/docs/index.html In the viewer, pick a sequence, click Load sequence, optionally Align sequence, then scrub the distance or press Play. To bake interpolated and extrapolated steps:
python -m alignment.bake --sequence-id cartboard-raw-normal-s60-200g --pack python -m alignment.bake --all --pack To rebuild the dataset from PNG maps or extract images:
python generate_datasets.py parquet --input-dir wear --output-dir data/parquet python generate_datasets.py webdataset --input-dir wear --output-dir data/shards python read_datasets.py decompress --shards-dir data/shards --output-dir data/images --workers 4 Repository guide data/parquet/ holds the Parquet leaves, sequences.json and metadata.parquet. data/shards/ holds the WebDataset .tar shards. metadata.json describes the materials, grits, loads, distances, capture setup and map types. alignment/ contains registration, warping, interpolation, extrapolation, baking and packing. docs/index.html, docs/serve_local.py and docs/serve_app.py are the viewer and its local servers. docs/prepare_viewer_parquets.py rebuilds sequences.json. docs/package/ vendors the parquet-wasm build used by the viewer. examples/Wear/powerpoint/ holds one PowerPoint deck per test series (cardboard, foam, MDF, PLA, sandpaper, soft wood). Features Wear sequences indexed by material, path shape, direction, grit, load and sliding distance. Two storage formats: nested Parquet for browsing and WebDataset shards for streaming. In-browser viewer with distance scrubbing, playback and prefetching of adjacent steps. Server-side SIFT/ECC alignment with cached results and a flat atlas download. Catmull-Rom interpolation and FFT plus SLERP extrapolation of normal maps. CLI tools to rebuild, extract and describe the dataset. Limits Parquet and shard files are Git LFS objects: a plain clone only contains pointers until git lfs pull runs. The wear/ PNG source tree used by generate_datasets.py is not in the repository, and data/aligned/ and data/wear_extrapolated/ are gitignored. The README and metadata.json name Alu and Resin, but the committed sequences.json has no Alu or Resin sequence. Extrapolated frames are model output, not measurements. Several sequences are short (two steps for some PLA and MDF series), and one foam folder is named 4000000mm. docs/README.md and metadata.json give different capture figures (resolution, number of LEDs, temperature), so treat them as descriptive. On a static host the viewer still loads frames, but alignment is disabled because it needs the Python server. There are no automated tests.
